Prompt Caching = feature that speeds up Claude's responses and reduces text generation costs by reusing computational work from previous requests.

Normal request flow: User sends message → Claude processes input (creates internal data structures, performs calculations) → Claude generates output → Claude discards all processing work → Ready for next request.

Problem: When follow-up requests contain identical input messages, Claude must repeat all the same computational work it just threw away, creating inefficiency.

Solution: Prompt caching stores the results of input message processing in temporary cache instead of discarding. When identical input appears in subsequent requests, Claude retrieves cached work rather than reprocessing, dramatically speeding response generation.

Key benefit: Reuses previous computational work to avoid redundant processing of repeated content.

Prompt Caching = system that saves processing work from initial request to reuse in follow-up requests with identical content

Core mechanism: Initial request → Claude processes + saves work to cache → Follow-up requests with identical content → Claude retrieves cached work instead of reprocessing

Cache duration = 1 hour maximum

Cache activation requires manual cache breakpoint addition to message blocks

Text block formats: - Shorthand: content = "text string" (cannot add cache control) - Longhand: content = [{"type": "text", "text": "content", "cache_control": {...}}] (required for caching)

Cache scope = all content up to and including breakpoint gets cached

Cache invalidation = any change in content before breakpoint invalidates entire cache

Content processing order = tools → system prompt → messages (joined together)

Cache breakpoint placement options: - Tool schemas - System prompts - Message blocks (text, image, tool use, tool result)

Maximum breakpoints = 4 per request

Multiple breakpoints = create multiple cache layers, partial cache hits possible if only later content changes

Minimum cache threshold = 1024 tokens required for content to be cached

Best use cases = repeated identical content (system prompts, tool definitions, static message prefixes)

Prompt Caching Implementation = automatically caches tool schemas and system prompts to reduce token usage

Setup = modify chat function to enable caching by default for tools and system prompts

Tool Schema Caching = add cache_control field with type "ephemeral" to last tool in list. Best practice: create copy of tools list, clone last tool schema, add cache control, then overwrite to avoid modifying original schemas

System Prompt Caching = wrap system prompt in text block dictionary with cache_control type "ephemeral"

Multiple Cache Breakpoints = can set cache points for both tools and system prompt in single request

Cache Order = tools → system prompt → messages

Token Usage Patterns: - cache_creation_input_tokens = tokens written to cache on first use - cache_read_input_tokens = tokens retrieved from cache on subsequent identical requests - Partial cache reads possible when some content matches cached data

Cache Invalidation = any change to cached content (tools or system prompt) invalidates cache, forces new cache creation

Use Cases = identical content across requests - same tool schemas, system prompts, or message sequences

Files API = allows uploading files ahead of time and referencing them later via file ID instead of including raw file data in each request. Upload file → get file metadata object with ID → use ID in future requests.

Code Execution = server-based tool where Claude executes Python code in isolated Docker containers. No implementation needed, just include predefined tool schema. Claude can run code multiple times, interpret results, generate final response.

Key constraints: Docker containers have no network access. Data input/output relies on Files API integration.

Combined workflow: Upload file via Files API → get file ID → include ID in container upload block → ask Claude to analyze → Claude writes/executes code with access to uploaded file → returns analysis and results.

Claude can generate files (plots, reports) inside container that can be downloaded using file IDs returned in response.

Use cases: Data analysis, file processing, automated code generation for complex tasks. Response contains code blocks, execution results, and final analysis.

Implementation: Use container upload block with file ID, include analysis prompt, Claude handles code execution automatically.

MCP = Model Context Protocol, communication layer providing Claude with context and tools without requiring developers to write tedious code.

Architecture: MCP client connects to MCP server. Server contains tools, resources, and prompts as internal components.

Problem solved: Eliminates burden of authoring/maintaining numerous tool schemas and functions for service integrations. Example: GitHub chatbot would require implementing tools for repositories, pull requests, issues, projects - significant developer effort.

Solution: MCP server handles tool definition and execution instead of your application server. MCP servers = interfaces to outside services, wrapping functionality into ready-to-use tools.

Key benefits: Developers avoid writing tool schemas and function implementations themselves.

Common questions: - Who creates MCP servers? Anyone, often service providers make official implementations (AWS, etc.) - vs direct API calls? MCP eliminates need to author tool schemas/functions yourself - vs tool use? MCP and tool use are complementary - MCP handles WHO does the work (server vs developer), both still involve tools

Core value: Shifts integration burden from application developers to MCP server maintainers.

MCP Client = communication interface between your server and MCP server, provides access to server's tools

Transport agnostic = client/server can communicate via multiple protocols (stdio, HTTP, WebSockets)

Common setup = client and server on same machine using standard input/output

Communication = message exchange defined by MCP spec

Key message types: - list tools request = client asks server for available tools - list tools result = server responds with tool list - call tool request = client asks server to run tool with arguments - call tool result = server responds with tool execution result

Typical flow: 1. User queries server 2. Server requests tool list from MCP client 3. MCP client sends list tools request to MCP server 4. MCP server responds with list tools result 5. Server sends query + tools to Claude 6. Claude requests tool execution 7. Server asks MCP client to run tool 8. MCP client sends call tool request to MCP server 9. MCP server executes tool (e.g. GitHub API call) 10. Results flow back through chain: MCP server → MCP client → server → Claude → user

Purpose = enables servers to delegate tool execution to specialized MCP servers while maintaining Claude integration

CLI-based chatbot project = teaches MCP client-server interaction through hands-on implementation

Project components: - MCP client = connects to custom MCP server - MCP server = provides 2 tools (read document, update document) - Document collection = fake documents stored in memory only

Key distinction: Normal projects implement either client OR server, not both. This project implements both for educational purposes.

Setup process: 1. Download CLI_project.zip starter code 2. Extract and open in code editor 3. Follow readme.md setup directions 4. Add API key to .env file 5. Install dependencies (with/without UV) 6. Run project: "uv run main.py" or "python main.py" 7. Test with chat prompt

Expected outcome = working chat interface that responds to basic queries, ready for MCP feature additions.

MCP server implementation using Python SDK creates tools through decorators rather than manual JSON schemas.

MCP Python SDK = Official package that auto-generates tool JSON schemas from Python function definitions using @mcp.tool decorator.

Tool definition syntax = @mcp.tool(name="tool_name", description="description") + function with typed parameters using Field() for argument descriptions.

Two tools implemented: 1. read_doc_contents = Takes doc_id string, returns document content from in-memory docs dictionary 2. edit_document = Takes doc_id, old_string, new_string parameters, performs find/replace on document content

Error handling = Check if doc_id exists in docs dictionary, raise ValueError if not found.

Key advantage = SDK eliminates manual JSON schema writing, generates schemas automatically from Python function signatures and decorators.

Required imports = Field from pydantic for parameter descriptions, mcp package for server and tool decorators.

Implementation pattern = Decorator defines tool metadata, function parameters define tool arguments with types and descriptions, function body contains tool logic.

MCP Inspector = in-browser debugger for testing MCP servers without connecting to applications

Access: Run `mcp dev [server_file.py]` in terminal → opens server on port → navigate to provided URL in browser

Interface: Left sidebar has connect button → top menu shows resources/prompts/tools sections → tools section lists available tools → click tool to open right panel for manual testing

Testing workflow: Connect to server → navigate to tools → select specific tool → input required parameters → click run tool → verify output

Key features: Live development testing, manual tool invocation, parameter input forms, success/failure feedback, no need for full application integration

Note: UI actively changing during development, core functionality remains similar

Example usage: Test document tools by inputting document IDs, verify read operations, test edit operations, chain operations to verify changes

Primary benefit: Debug MCP server implementations efficiently during development phase

MCP Client Implementation:

MCP Client = wrapper class around client session for resource cleanup and connection management to MCP server

Client Session = actual connection to MCP server from MCP Python SDK, requires resource cleanup on close

Client Purpose = exposes MCP server functionality to rest of codebase, enables reaching out to server for tool lists and tool execution

Key Functions: - list_tools() = await self.session.list_tools(), return result.tools - call_tool() = await self.session.call_tool(tool_name, tool_input)

Usage Flow = client gets tool definitions to send to Claude, then executes tools when Claude requests them

Common Pattern = wrap client session in larger class for resource management rather than use session directly

Testing = can run client file directly with testing harness to verify server connection and tool retrieval

Integration = other code in project calls client functions to interact with MCP server, enabling Claude to inspect/edit documents through defined tools

MCP Resources = mechanism allowing MCP servers to expose data to clients for read operations

Resource Types = 2 types: direct (static URI like "docs://documents") and templated (parameterized URI like "docs://documents/{doc_id}")

URI = address/identifier for accessing specific resource, defined when creating resource

Resource Flow = client sends read resource request with URI → server matches URI to function → server executes function → returns data in read resource result

Implementation = use @mcp.resource decorator with URI and MIME type parameters

MIME Types = hint to client about returned data format (application/json for structured data, text/plain for plain text)

Templated Resources = URI parameters automatically parsed by SDK and passed as keyword arguments to handler function

Resource vs Tools = resources provide data proactively (fetch document contents when @ mentioned), tools perform actions reactively (when Claude decides to call them)

Data Return = SDK automatically serializes returned data to strings, client responsible for deserialization

Testing = MCP inspector can list direct resources separately from templated resources, allows testing individual resource calls

MCP Resource Access Implementation:

Resource Reading Function = client-side function to request and parse resources from MCP server

Function Parameters = URI (resource identifier)

Implementation Steps: - Import json module + AnyURL from pydantic - Call await self.session.read_resource(AnyURL(uri)) - Extract first element from result.contents[0] - Check resource.mime_type for parsing strategy

Content Parsing Logic: - If mime_type == "application/json" → return json.loads(resource.text) - Otherwise → return resource.text (plain text)

Server Response Structure = result.contents list with first element containing type/mime_type metadata

Resource Integration = MCP client functions called by other application components to fetch document contents for prompts

End Result = Document contents automatically included in Claude prompts without requiring tool calls

Key Point = Resources expose server information directly to clients through structured request/response pattern

MCP Prompts = Pre-defined, tested prompt templates that MCP servers expose to client applications for specialized tasks.

Purpose = Instead of users writing ad-hoc prompts, server authors create high-quality, evaluated prompts tailored to their server's domain.

Implementation = Use @mcpserver.prompt decorator with name/description, define function that returns list of messages (user/assistant messages that can be sent directly to Claude).

Example Use Case = Document formatting prompt that takes document ID, instructs Claude to read document using tools, reformat to markdown, and save changes.

Key Benefits = Server-specific expertise, pre-tested quality, reusable across client applications, better results than user-generated prompts.

Message Structure = Returns base.UserMessage objects containing the formatted prompt text with interpolated parameters.

Client Integration = Prompts appear as autocomplete options (slash commands) in client applications, prompt user for required parameters, then execute the pre-built prompt workflow.

MCP Client Prompt Implementation:

List prompts = await self.session.list_prompts(), return result.prompts Get prompt = await self.session.get_prompt(prompt_name, arguments), return result.messages

Prompt workflow: 1. Define prompt in MCP server with expected arguments (e.g., document_id) 2. Client calls get_prompt with prompt name + arguments dictionary 3. Arguments passed as keyword arguments to prompt function 4. Function interpolates arguments into prompt text 5. Returns messages array for direct feeding to LLM

Key concept: Prompts are server-defined templates that clients can invoke with specific arguments to generate contextualized instructions for LLMs. Arguments flow from client call → prompt function → interpolated prompt text → LLM consumption.

Anthropic Apps = two deployed applications by Anthropic: Claude Code and Computer Use.

Claude Code = terminal-based coding assistant that serves as example of agent architecture.

Computer Use = toolset that expands Claude's capabilities beyond text generation.

Key purpose = these apps demonstrate agent concepts and provide practical examples for understanding agent design and implementation.

Setup process = involves terminal configuration for Claude Code usage on sample projects.

Agent connection = both applications exemplify how agents work, serving as learning models for building effective agents.

Claude Code = terminal-based coding assistant program that helps with code-related tasks

Core capabilities = search/read/edit files + advanced tools (web fetching, terminal access) + MCP client support for expanded functionality via MCP servers

Setup process: 1. Install Node.js (check with "npm help" command) 2. Run npm install to install Claude Code 3. Execute "claude" command in terminal to login to Anthropic account

Full setup guide = docs.anthropic.com

MCP client functionality = can consume tools from MCP servers to extend capabilities beyond basic file operations

Claude Code = AI coding assistant that functions as a collaborative engineer on projects, not just a code generator.

Key capabilities: project setup, feature design, code writing, testing, deployment, error fixing in production.

Setup workflow: - Download project, open in editor - Run `claude` command to launch - Ask Claude to read README and execute setup directions - Run `init` command = Claude scans codebase for architecture/coding style, creates claude.md file - claude.md = automatically included context for future requests

Memory types: Project (shared), Local, User memory files.

Context management: - Use # symbol to add specific notes to memory - Can manually edit claude.md or rerun init to update - Claude can handle Git operations (staging, committing)

Effective prompting strategies:

Method 1 - Three-step workflow: 1. Identify relevant files, ask Claude to analyze them 2. Describe feature, ask Claude to plan solution (no code yet) 3. Ask Claude to implement the plan

Method 2 - Test-driven development: 1. Provide relevant context 2. Ask Claude to suggest tests for the feature 3. Select and implement chosen tests 4. Ask Claude to write code until tests pass

Core principle: Claude Code = effort multiplier. More detailed instructions = significantly better results. Treat as collaborative engineer, not just code generator.

Claude Code = AI assistant with embedded MCP (Model Context Protocol) client that can connect to MCP servers to expand functionality.

MCP Server Integration = Connect external tools/services to Claude Code via command: `claude mcp add [server-name] [startup-command]`

Example Implementation = Document processing server exposing "Document Path to Markdown" tool, allowing Claude Code to read PDF/Word documents by running `uv run main.py`

Dynamic Capability Expansion = MCP servers add new functions to Claude Code in real-time without core modifications.

Common Use Cases = Production monitoring (Sentry), project management (Jira), communication (Slack), custom development workflow tools.

Key Benefit = Significant flexibility increase for development workflows through modular server connections.

Setup Process = 1) Create MCP server with tools, 2) Add server to Claude Code with name and startup command, 3) Restart Claude Code to access new capabilities.

Parallelizing Claude Code = running multiple Claude instances simultaneously to complete different tasks in parallel

Core Problem = multiple Claude instances modifying same files simultaneously creates conflicts and invalid code

Solution = Git work trees providing isolated workspaces per Claude instance

Git Work Trees = feature creating complete project copies in separate directories, each corresponding to different Git branches

Workflow = create work tree → assign task to Claude instance → work in isolation → commit changes → merge back to main branch

Custom Commands = automating work tree creation/management through .claude/commands directory with markdown files containing prompts

Command Structure = .claude/commands/filename.md with $ARGUMENTS placeholder for dynamic values

Parallel Execution Benefits = single developer commanding virtual team of software engineers, major productivity scaling limited only by engineer's management capacity

Merge Conflicts = Claude automatically resolves conflicts during branch merging process

Cleanup = Claude handles work tree removal after feature completion

Key Advantage = scales to unlimited parallel instances based on developer's capacity to manage simultaneous tasks

Automated Debugging = using AI (Claude) to automatically detect, analyze, and fix production errors without manual intervention.

Core Workflow: 1. GitHub Action runs daily to check production environment 2. Fetches CloudWatch logs from last 24 hours 3. Claude identifies errors, deduplicates them 4. Claude analyzes each error and generates fixes 5. Creates pull request with proposed solutions

Key Components: - GitHub Actions for scheduling/automation - AWS CLI for log retrieval - Claude Code for error analysis and code fixes - CloudWatch for production error monitoring

Benefits: - Catches production-only errors (issues not present in development) - Reduces manual log hunting and debugging time - Provides context-aware fixes with explanations - Creates reviewable pull requests for changes

Common Use Case: Configuration errors between environments (invalid model IDs, API keys, etc. that work locally but fail in production)

Implementation Requirements: Repository access, cloud logging service, AI coding assistant, CI/CD pipeline integration.

Computer Use = Claude's ability to interact with computer interfaces through visual observation and control actions.

Key capabilities: - Takes screenshots of applications/browsers - Clicks buttons, types text, navigates interfaces - Follows multi-step instructions autonomously - Performs QA testing and automation tasks

How it works: - Runs in isolated Docker container environment - User provides instructions via chat interface - Claude observes screen visually and executes actions - Generates reports on task completion/results

Primary use cases: - Automated QA testing of web applications - UI interaction testing across different scenarios - Time-saving for repetitive computer tasks - Bug identification through systematic testing

Setup requirement = Reference implementation available for local testing

Example workflow: User describes testing requirements → Claude navigates to application → Executes test cases → Reports pass/fail results with detailed findings

Computer use = tool system implementation allowing Claude to interact with computing environments

Tool use flow: User sends message + tool schema → Claude responds with tool use request (ID, name, input) → Server executes code → Result sent back to Claude as tool result

Computer use follows identical flow: - Special tool schema sent to Claude (small schema expands to larger structure behind scenes) - Expanded schema includes action function with arguments: mouse move, left click, screenshot, etc. - Claude sends tool use request - Developers must fulfill request via computing environment (typically Docker container) - Container executes programmatic key presses/mouse movements - Response sent back to Claude

Key points: - Claude doesn't directly manipulate computers - Computer use = tool system + developer-provided computing environment - Anthropic provides reference implementation (Docker container with pre-built mouse/keyboard execution code) - Setup requires Docker + simple command execution - Enables direct chat interface for testing Claude's computer use functionality

Computer use = abstraction layer where tool system handles Claude communication while Docker container handles actual computer interactions.

Workflows and agents = strategies for handling user tasks that can't be completed by Claude in a single request.

Decision rule: Use workflows when you have precise task understanding and know exact steps sequence. Use agents when task details are unclear.

Workflow = series of calls to Claude for specific problems where steps are predetermined.

Example workflow: Image to 3D model converter - Step 1: Claude describes uploaded image in detail - Step 2: Claude uses CADQuery Python library to model object from description - Step 3: Create rendering of model - Step 4: Claude compares rendering to original image - Step 5: If inaccurate, repeat from step 2 with feedback

This follows evaluator-optimizer pattern: - Producer = generates output (Claude + CADQuery modeling) - Evaluator = assesses output quality (comparison step) - Loop continues until evaluator accepts output

Key point: Workflows are implementation patterns that other engineers have successfully used. Identifying workflow patterns doesn't automatically implement them - you still need to write the actual code.

Parallelization Workflows = breaking one complex task into multiple simultaneous subtasks, then aggregating results.

Example: Material selection for parts - Instead of: One large prompt asking Claude to choose between metal/polymer/ceramic/composite with all criteria - Use: Separate parallel requests, each evaluating one material's suitability, then final aggregation step to compare results

Structure: Input → Multiple parallel subtasks → Aggregator → Final output

Benefits: - Focus = Each subtask handles one specific analysis instead of juggling multiple considerations - Modularity = Individual prompts can be improved/evaluated separately - Scalability = Easy to add new subtasks without affecting existing ones - Quality = Reduces confusion from overly complex single prompts

Key principle: Decompose complex decisions into specialized parallel analyses, then synthesize results.

Chaining Workflows = breaking large tasks into series of distinct sequential steps rather than single complex prompt

Core concept: Instead of one massive prompt with multiple requirements, split into separate calls where each focuses on one specific subtask.

Example workflow: User enters topic → search trending topics → Claude selects most interesting → Claude researches topic → Claude writes script → generate video → post to social media

Key benefit: Allows AI to focus on individual tasks rather than juggling multiple constraints simultaneously

Primary use case: When Claude consistently ignores constraints in complex prompts despite repetition. Common with long prompts containing many "don't do X" requirements.

Problem scenario: Long prompt with constraints (don't mention AI, no emojis, professional tone) → Claude violates some constraints regardless of repetition

Solution: Step 1 - Send initial prompt, accept imperfect output. Step 2 - Follow-up prompt asking Claude to rewrite based on specific violations found.

Critical insight: Even simple-seeming workflow becomes essential when dealing with constraint-heavy prompts that AI struggles to follow completely in single pass.

Routing Workflows = workflow pattern that categorizes user input to determine appropriate processing pipeline

Key mechanism: Initial request to Claude categorizes user input into predefined genres/categories. Based on categorization response, system routes to specialized processing pipeline with customized prompts/tools.

Example flow: 1. User enters topic (e.g., "Python functions") 2. Claude categorizes topic (e.g., "educational") 3. System uses educational-specific prompt template 4. Claude generates script with educational tone/structure

Benefits: Ensures output matches topic nature. Programming topics get educational treatment with definitions/explanations. Entertainment topics get trendy language/engaging hooks.

Structure: One routing step → Multiple specialized processing pipelines → Each pipeline has customized prompts/tools for specific category

Use case: Social media video script generation where different topics require different tones and approaches.

Agents = AI systems that create plans to complete tasks using provided tools, effective when exact steps are unknown. Workflows = better when precise steps are known.

Key differences: Workflows require predetermined steps, agents dynamically plan using available tools.

Agent advantages: Flexibility to solve variety of tasks with same toolset, can combine tools in unexpected ways.

Tool abstraction principle: Provide generic/abstract tools rather than hyper-specialized ones. Example - Claude code uses bash, web_fetch, file_write (abstract) rather than refactor_tool, install_dependencies (specialized).

Tool combination examples: get_current_datetime + add_duration + set_reminder can solve various time-related tasks through different combinations.

Agent behavior: Can request additional information when needed, combines tools creatively to achieve goals, works best with small set of flexible tools.

Design approach: Give agent abstract tools that can be pieced together rather than single-purpose specialized tools. This enables dynamic problem-solving and unexpected use cases.

Environment Inspection = agents evaluating their environment and action results to understand progress and handle errors.

Core concept: After each action, agents need feedback mechanisms beyond basic tool returns to understand new environment state.

Computer use example: Claude takes screenshot after every action (typing, clicking) to see how environment changed, since it cannot predict exact results of actions like button clicks.

Code editing example: Before modifying files, agents must read current file contents to understand existing state.

Social media video agent applications: - Use Whisper CPP via bash to generate timestamped captions, verify dialogue placement - Use FFmpeg to extract video screenshots at intervals, inspect visual results - Validate video creation meets expectations before posting

Key benefit: Environment inspection enables agents to gauge task progress, detect errors, and adapt to unexpected results rather than operating blindly.

Workflows = pre-defined series of calls to Claude with known exact steps. Agents = flexible approach using basic tools that Claude combines to complete unknown tasks.

Key differences:

Task division: Workflows break big tasks into smaller, specific subtasks enabling higher focus and accuracy. Agents handle varied challenges creatively without predetermined steps.

Testing/evaluation: Workflows easier to test due to known execution sequence. Agents harder to test since execution path unpredictable.

User experience: Workflows require specific inputs. Agents create own inputs from user queries and can request additional input when needed.

Success rates: Workflows = higher task completion rates due to structured approach. Agents = lower completion rates due to delegated complexity.

Recommendation: Prioritize workflows for reliability. Use agents only when flexibility truly required. Users want 100% working products over fancy agents.

Core principle: Solve problems reliably first, innovation second.

docs.title: Module 06 — Learning Anything with AI
docs.text:
Goal: use Claude (plus a source-grounded research notebook such as Gemini NotebookLM) to learn a new topic fast without letting AI do the learning for you.

# Lesson Time 1 Be the client, not the audience 5 min 2 Stage 1 — Collect: build a library you can trust 15 min 3 Stage 2 — Understand: ask, focus, reshape 15 min 4 Stage 3 — Own: an archive your future self can use 15 min

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph C["1 · Collect"]
        C1[Brief] --> C2[Deep research] --> C3[Audit sources] --> C4[Curated library]
    end
    subgraph U["2 · Understand"]
        U1[Ask] --> U2[Focus] --> U3[Reshape]
    end
    subgraph O["3 · Own"]
        O1[Keep questions,<br/>artifacts, links] --> O2[Archive with index] --> O3[Retrieve later]
    end
    C --> U --> O

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
Role Tool Job 🧑‍💼 You — the client — Set direction, decide what deserves attention, make the final judgment 🧠 Consultant Claude (or any chatbot you prefer) Plan, write prompts, audit sources, reshape answers, design the archive 📚 Librarian / library Research notebook (e.g. Gemini NotebookLM) Gather sources, hold the library, answer grounded in it 🗂️ Archivist Claude with folder access (desktop app / Claude Code) Build and maintain the folder archive

Speed comes from the tools. Quality comes from you: how you direct them, the context you give, and what you choose to keep.

docs.title: How this connects to the rest of the course
docs.text:
• Collect uses three-part prompting and plan-mode-style questioning.
  • Understand uses Claude to build interactive pages, which are the same kind of artifacts covered in Module 05.
  • Own uses folder access, CLAUDE.md-style index files, and optionally a skill to file new sessions.

➡️ Practice: Lab 09 — Learning workflow · Template: examples/learning-archive/

docs.title: 1. Be the Client, Not the Audience
docs.text:
AI can now run almost the entire learning process itself: it finds sources, summarizes them, explains them and builds slides. The trap is that you end up watching AI learn for you. That gets you answers faster, but you haven't learned anything faster.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Audience["👀 Audience mode"]
        A1[Ask AI] --> A2[Read the output] --> A3[Forget it]
    end
    subgraph Client["🧑‍💼 Client mode"]
        B1[Set goal & context] --> B2[Direct the tools]
        B2 --> B3[Audit & choose focus]
        B3 --> B4[Reshape for yourself]
        B4 --> B5[Keep what matters]
    end

docs.title: The client's responsibilities
docs.text: You decide… Why it matters The goal and context Shapes every prompt in the workflow Which sources to trust AI-gathered sources often contain SEO marketing, duplicates or fabricated entries Which questions deserve attention Prevents a generic, scattered summary What form helps you understand A table, a deck, an interactive map, whatever works for how you read What to keep Your archive is an index of your thinking, not of everything AI produced

docs.title: Save mental energy for the parts that matter
docs.text:
Let AI do the work your brain doesn't need to do, such as drafting prompts, collecting sources and reformatting. Then spend your attention on judgment.

pie showData
    title Where your attention should go
    "Choosing focus & judging" : 60
    "Reviewing AI drafts" : 30
    "Writing prompts from scratch" : 5
    "Manual searching & formatting" : 5

➡️ Next: Stage 1 — Collect

docs.title: 2. Stage 1 — Collect: Build a Library You Can Trust
docs.text:
Goal: a curated set of sources that you've checked, collected without exhausting yourself before the real learning starts.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant You
    participant Claude as Claude (consultant)
    participant NB as Research notebook (library)
    You->>Claude: Topic + 4-part context
    Claude-->>You: Draft research prompt
    You->>You: Trim over-prompting
    You->>NB: Prompt in deep-research mode
    NB-->>You: ~60–70 sources
    You->>NB: "Extract all sources into a Markdown file"
    NB-->>You: sources.md (+ its own self-diagnosis)
    You->>Claude: sources.md → "audit this"
    Claude-->>You: Duplicates, suspected fabrications, wrong focus, missing sources
    You->>Claude: Keep / drop decisions
    Claude-->>You: Final list (~30)
    You->>NB: New notebook from the final list
    Note over NB: ✅ Verified library

docs.title: Step 1 — Write the brief with Claude
docs.text:
Don't write the research prompt from zero. Give Claude the four things every research brief needs and ask it to draft the prompt:

Context item Example 🎯 Goal "Compare prompt, context, harness and loop engineering to decide how to design my test agent" 📏 Depth "Practitioner-level, not academic; enough to make design decisions" 🧑 Background "Automotive test engineer, strong Python, built RAG systems, new to agent harnesses" ✅ Good sources "Official docs, engineering blogs from labs, papers, talks by practitioners. No listicles, no vendor comparisons"

Template: examples/learning-archive/templates/research-brief.md

⚠️ AI tends to over-prompt. Read the draft and cut anything that doesn't serve your goal.

docs.title: Step 2 — Deep research in the notebook
docs.text: Paste the prompt into the research notebook, run its deep research mode, and remove sources that failed to load.

docs.title: Step 3 — Audit (especially for fast-moving topics)
docs.text:
Nobody reads 60+ sources. You either trust the list or audit it.

flowchart TD
    Q{Is the topic new<br/>or moving fast?}
    Q -->|Yes| A[Audit with a second AI]
    Q -->|No, well established| T[Trusting is usually OK]
    A --> E["Export sources to Markdown"]
    E --> C[Claude reviews the list]

Ask Claude to look for problems like these:

Problem Example from the video Duplicates Same article from two URLs Possibly fabricated sources Titles or authors that don't seem to exist Wrong focus Many "10 best MCP gateways" articles, which are SEO marketing that would pull the whole synthesis toward vendor comparison Gaps Important primary sources that are missing, which Claude can suggest

The research notebook's own self-check flagged different problems than the second AI did. That's why a second opinion is worth having.

docs.title: Audit prompt
docs.text:
Here is a source list for research on <topic>. My goal: <goal>.
Audit it: flag duplicates, possibly fabricated or unverifiable sources,
marketing/SEO content, and anything that would skew the focus away from
my goal. Suggest up to 5 missing high-quality sources.
Output a table: source | keep/drop | reason.

docs.title: Step 4 — Rebuild a clean notebook
docs.text:
Create a new notebook from only the kept sources. In the video this took under 5 minutes and went from 64 sources to about 30.

✅ Outcome: a verified library, and you still have the energy for Stage 2.

➡️ Next: Stage 2 — Understand

docs.title: 3. Stage 2 — Understand: Ask, Focus, Reshape
docs.text: AI explains brilliantly. It can turn a pile of text into a summary, report or deck faster than you can absorb it. So the output itself matters less than the choices you make around it.

docs.title: The mini loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Ask["❓ Ask<br/>Claude proposes questions<br/>from your goal"] --> Focus["🎯 Focus<br/>you compress them to the few<br/>that deserve attention"]
    Focus --> Answer["📚 Answer<br/>notebook answers each one<br/>grounded in the library"]
    Answer --> Reshape["🔁 Reshape<br/>turn answers into a form<br/>that helps YOU understand"]
    Reshape -.new questions.-> Ask

docs.title: Ask → Focus
docs.text:
Tell Claude your purpose and goal and let it suggest questions. In the video Claude produced six blocks of questions. Don't copy them blindly. Compress them into a small "attention zone" of about five questions that you actually care about.

My goal: <goal>. My background: <background>.
Suggest the questions I should answer to reach this goal, grouped by theme.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Ask the notebook your questions one at a time, so each answer is grounded in your curated library.

docs.title: Reshape: pick the right format
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{What do you need?}
    Q -->|Fast overview of dense,<br/>technical material| T[📊 Data table<br/>notebook studio]
    Q -->|A different structure /<br/>new perspective| S[🖼️ Slide deck<br/>notebook studio]
    Q -->|Something specific to MY problem,<br/>many moving parts| C[🧩 Interactive page<br/>built by Claude]
    Q -->|Hard to read long reports<br/>accessibility, 2nd language| G[🕸️ Context graph +<br/>reading hub, built by Claude]
Format Tool Best for Data table Notebook studio output Condensing dense technical material without getting overwhelmed Slide deck Notebook studio output Seeing the same information in another structure Interactive page Claude Applying concepts to your specific problem Context graph + reading hub Claude Navigating a long report visually: the map shows structure, the hub gives detail

💡 Generate decks from your answers, not the whole library. If you use the whole library, the notebook decides what matters and you get a generic summary. Your answers already reflect your focus.

docs.title: Example: when text answers stop working
docs.text:
Question: "For one specific task, how does the setup change across prompt, context, harness and loop design?"

The prompt and context layers are easy to follow in text. The harness and loop layers bring in tools, agents and feedback, and become hard to hold in your head. So ask Claude to reshape the answer into an interactive page:

flowchart TB
    subgraph L1[Prompt layer]
        P1[System prompt] --> P2[Task instructions]
    end
    subgraph L2[Context layer]
        C1[Skill file] --> C2[Retrieved docs]
        C2 --> C3[Memory]
    end
    subgraph L3[Harness layer]
        H1[Tools] --> H2[Error channel]
        H2 --> H3[Agent]
    end
    subgraph L4[Loop layer]
        R1[Run] --> R2[Evaluate] --> R3[Feedback] --> R1
    end
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4

On the page, every box can be clicked to reveal a concrete example: what the skill file contains, or what an error message looks like when it flows back to the agent. Each abstract concept is tied to something concrete.

Here are my answers on <topic>. Reshape them into an interactive page
around MY task: <task>. Show each layer as a workflow; clicking a box
should reveal a concrete example (file contents, message format, etc.).

➡️ Next: Stage 3 — Own

docs.title: 4. Stage 3 — Own: An Archive Your Future Self Can Use
docs.text: Learning something is only the beginning. To own it, you need to capture, organize and retrieve it when you need it. Claude with folder access acts as your librarian: it designs and maintains a folder system on your computer.

docs.title: Decide what's worth keeping
docs.text:
The archive is an index of your own thinking, not a dump of everything AI produced.

Keep Why ❓ Your questions They show the path your thinking took 🧩 Artifacts you chose to develop They capture the parts you went deeper on 🔗 Notebook link Gets you back to the original sources

Success test: "If I come back to this topic in 3 weeks, can I see what I learned, how far I got, and get back to the sources?"

docs.title: Give Claude the material and the job, not the structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    M["📥 Material<br/>questions.md exported from notebook<br/>+ chosen artifacts<br/>in one folder"] --> Claude
    J["🎯 Job<br/>how you'll USE the archive later"] --> Claude
    Claude --> P[Proposed structure + logic]
    P -->|you approve| B[Claude builds it]

Describe how you will use the archive, not which folders to create. The structure follows from the use.

This folder contains my learning material. I want an archive I can come
back to weeks later and ask things like "what did I learn about X?",
"what did I learn in June?", or "show all my questions about Y".
For each session I keep: my questions, the artifacts I chose, and a link
to the research notebook. Propose a structure and the logic behind it,
explain how it scales, and put anything you're unsure about in an inbox
instead of guessing. Don't build until I approve.

docs.title: The resulting structure (as in the video)
docs.text:
learning-archive/
├── INDEX.md                         ← top-level index, written for AI to read
├── inbox/                           ← anything Claude wasn't sure how to file
└── sessions/
    └── 2026-10-24_ai-agent-engineering/
        ├── SESSION.md               ← notebook link, tags, file list, summary
        ├── questions.md             ← the questions, in the order asked
        └── artifacts/
            └── layer-explorer.html

flowchart TB
    I[INDEX.md<br/>all sessions, tags, dates] --> S1[SESSION.md<br/>2026-10-24 AI agents]
    I --> S2[SESSION.md<br/>2026-11-xx next topic]
    S1 --> Q[questions.md]
    S1 --> A[artifacts/]
    S1 --> N[🔗 notebook]
    Inbox[inbox/] -.->|filed when clear| I
  • One folder per learning session, named YYYY-MM-DD_topic.
  • INDEX.md and SESSION.md are written mainly for AI. They tell Claude where the notebook lives and which files belong to which session, so it can answer without opening every artifact.
  • Inbox, not guessing. Uncertain items wait for you.

Template: examples/learning-archive/

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
Open a chat with folder access to the archive and ask:

What did I learn about AI agents?

Claude finds the session, reports its date and tags, shows the progression of your questions, links back to the notebook, and lists the artifacts without opening them.

Queries that become valuable once the archive grows: - "What did I learn in June?" - "Pull out every question I've asked about harness engineering." - "Which topics did I start but never go deep on?"

docs.title: Make it a habit (optional, using Module 03)
docs.text:
• Put the filing rules in a skill (/file-session) so every new session is archived the same way.
  • Add a CLAUDE.md to the archive with the conventions. The template includes one.
  • A monthly routine can tidy the inbox and refresh INDEX.md.

✅ Module complete. Head to Lab 09 or continue with 07 Running with Ollama.

docs.title: Module 07 — Running with Ollama
docs.text:
Goal: connect Claude Code to local and cloud open-weights models through Ollama's Anthropic-compatible API for private, offline, or alternative-model workflows.

# Lesson Time 1 Quickstart & setup 10 min 2 Selecting models & context 15 min 3 Headless automation & /loop 10 min 4 Cloud models & channels 10 min 5 Local model tactics & Storybook 15 min 6 CLI tools & Python SDK 10 min 7 Alternative providers & gateways 10 min

docs.title: How Ollama fits into Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code communicates using Anthropic's Messages API. Ollama provides an Anthropic-compatible API layer, allowing Claude Code to run against either local models running on your machine or Ollama Cloud models without changing how Claude Code works.

flowchart TD
    CC[Claude Code CLI / Desktop]

    subgraph Backends["Inference Backends"]
        direction TB
        Anthropic["☁️ Anthropic Cloud<br/>(Claude Opus / Sonnet / Haiku)"]
        OllamaLocal["💻 Local Ollama Daemon<br/>http://localhost:11434<br/>(Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek)"]
        OllamaCloud["🌐 Ollama Cloud<br/>https://ollama.com<br/>(Kimi, Gemma, GLM)"]
    end

    CC -->|Default| Anthropic
    CC -->|ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=localhost:11434| OllamaLocal
    CC -->|ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=ollama.com| OllamaCloud

    style OllamaLocal fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#43a047
    style OllamaCloud fill:#e0f7fa,stroke:#00838f
    style Anthropic fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#fb8c00

docs.title: Supported capabilities
docs.text: Capability Supported with Ollama Notes Chat & code reasoning ✅ Ask questions about codebases and architectures Command-line execution ✅ Runs build, test, and shell commands with standard permission checks Tool calling ✅ Works with compatible models (e.g. Qwen 2.5/3.5, Llama 3.3) File edits ✅ Reading, diffing, and writing files Subagents ✅ Delegating subtasks with separate context windows Web search & fetch ✅ Uses Ollama's web search API Vision ✅ Analyze images and UI screenshots with multimodal models Thinking ✅ Supported on thinking-enabled models Scheduled tasks ✅ Native /loop command for recurring prompts Channels ✅ Remote access via Telegram bot integration

docs.title: Why run with Ollama?
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["🔒 Complete Privacy<br/>Code never leaves your machine"] --> Y((Why Ollama?))
    B["💸 No Usage Caps<br/>Run unlimited queries locally"] --> Y
    C["✈️ Offline Work<br/>Code on flights or without internet"] --> Y
    D["🧪 Alternative Models<br/>Test Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, Gemma"] --> Y

Checkpoint: understand how to launch Claude Code with local models, configure environment variables, choose high-context models, and automate tasks with /loop.

➡️ Practice: Lab 10 — Ollama & Local Models

docs.title: 1. Quickstart & Setup
docs.text:
Ollama bridges Claude Code to open-source models using its Anthropic-compatible API. You can launch Claude Code with a single Ollama command or configure your terminal environment manually.

sequenceDiagram
    participant You
    participant CC as Claude Code CLI
    participant OL as Ollama (localhost:11434)
    participant M as Model (e.g. Qwen 3.5)

    You->>CC: claude --model qwen3.5
    CC->>OL: POST /v1/messages (Anthropic API format)
    OL->>M: Forward prompt + tools
    M-->>OL: Model response + tool calls
    OL-->>CC: Anthropic-formatted stream
    CC-->>You: File edits, command runs, answers

docs.title: Method 1: The One-Liner (ollama launch)
docs.text:
If you have Ollama installed, the fastest way to start is the ollama launch command:

ollama --version    # verify installation (e.g. 0.40+)
ollama list         # inspect currently downloaded models
ollama launch claude

What this command does automatically: 1. Verifies or downloads Claude Code. 2. Prompts you to pick a compatible local or cloud model (e.g. Qwen 2.5 Coder, Gemma, GLM). 3. Automatically sets the necessary API endpoints and auth tokens. 4. Spawns Claude Code directly in your current directory.

docs.title: Switching Models with --config
docs.text:
If you have multiple models installed or want to switch your active model without manually setting environment variables:

ollama launch claude --config

This opens an interactive menu allowing you to choose between your installed local models and cloud providers before launching.

To reset any saved integration profiles back to factory defaults: 

ollama launch claude --restore

docs.title: Workspace Safety Check
docs.text:
On your first launch in any folder, Claude Code will ask:

Quick safety check: is the current project created or one trusted like you own the code or well-known open source project?

Select Yes for your own projects to enable read, edit, and tool permissions.

docs.title: Automated Setup Script (setup-ollama.sh)
docs.text:
This tutorial includes an automated setup script in the repository root:

./setup-ollama.sh                  # Setup with default model (qwen2.5-coder:7b)
./setup-ollama.sh gpt-oss:20b-cloud # Setup with an existing or preferred model
./setup-ollama.sh --skip-pull      # Configure launcher without pulling new models

The script automatically verifies your environment, ensures the Ollama daemon is running on port 11434, tests inference, and generates a convenient ./launch-claude-ollama.sh launcher.

docs.title: Method 2: Manual Environment Variable Setup
docs.text: If you prefer using the standard claude CLI directly, install Claude Code and configure three environment variables.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Claude Code
docs.text:
macOS / Linux: 

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

Windows (PowerShell): 

irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

docs.title: Step 2: Set Environment Variables
docs.text:
Configure your shell to route requests to Ollama instead of Anthropic's servers:

export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434

Why empty ANTHROPIC_API_KEY? Clearing this ensures Claude Code does not attempt to authenticate against Anthropic's cloud with a stale Anthropic key, while ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN satisfies the client requirement for a bearer token.

docs.title: Step 3: Run Claude Code with your model
docs.text:
Launch Claude Code and specify which model Ollama should serve:

claude --model qwen3.5

You can also pass the variables inline for a single session without altering your shell profile:

ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama \
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434 \
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" \
claude --model kimi-k2.7-code:cloud

docs.title: Verifying the Connection
docs.text:
Once inside Claude Code, run the status slash command:

/status

Check the output for: - Model: shows the model name you specified (e.g. qwen3.5 or kimi-k2.7-code:cloud). - Base URL: confirms http://localhost:11434 is active.

> /status
Model: qwen3.5
API Base URL: http://localhost:11434
Context Window: 65,536 tokens

docs.title: Common Gotchas
docs.text:
Issue Cause Fix Connection refused Ollama daemon is not running Run ollama serve or open the Ollama desktop app Requests going to Anthropic Claude settings file overrides shell variables Check ~/.claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.json for fixed apiKey or baseUrl properties Model not found error Model hasn't been pulled locally yet Run ollama pull <model-name> first, or use ollama launch claude

➡️ Next: Selecting models & context

docs.title: 2. Selecting Models & Context
docs.text: Unlike standard chat applications, Claude Code is an agentic system. It continuously executes tools (reading files, parsing directory trees, running bash commands, editing code chunks). Because of this, two factors determine success with Ollama: tool-calling support and context length.

docs.title: 1. Tool-Calling Support is Mandatory
docs.text:
Not every model supports tool calling. If a model cannot reliably generate structured tool calls, Claude Code will fail to inspect files or execute commands.

flowchart TD
    M{Does the model support tool calling?}
    M -->|No| Fail["❌ Fails to read files, run bash, or edit code"]
    M -->|Yes| C{Context length >= 64k?}
    C -->|No| Trunc["⚠️ Context overflow on medium repositories"]
    C -->|Yes| Good["✅ Full Claude Code capabilities"]

    style Good fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#43a047
    style Fail fill:#ffebee,stroke:#e53935
    style Trunc fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#fbc02d

docs.title: Recommended Models
docs.text:
Model Type Best for Strengths Qwen 2.5 Coder / 3.5 (7B–32B) Local Local developer workstations Top-tier code edits, robust tool calling, fast Llama 3.1 / 3.3 (70B) Local / Cloud High-complexity reasoning Broad general knowledge, strong system adherence Kimi k2.7-code Cloud Large multi-file refactors Long context handling, strong tool calling Gemma 4 Cloud Lightweight tasks & scripts Fast inference, cost-effective GLM-5.3-flash Cloud Fast interactive development Quick response times, solid tool calling

Browse available models: - Local tool models: ollama.com/search?c=tools - Cloud models: ollama.com/search?c=cloud

docs.title: 2. The 64k+ Context Requirement
docs.text:
Claude Code sends substantial prompt overhead with every request: - System prompt and CLI behavior rules. - Tool schemas (read, edit, bash, subagent, grep, glob). - Project instructions from CLAUDE.md. - Project memory and active directory files.

[!NOTE] Default Ollama models often instantiate with a 2,048 or 4,096 token context window. In Claude Code, this fills up on the very first prompt. Always set a context window of 65,536 (64k) or higher.

docs.title: Configuring Context Length in Ollama
docs.text:
You can create a custom Modelfile with the context size configured:

# Modelfile
FROM qwen2.5-coder:14b

# Set 64k context window
PARAMETER num_ctx 65536

Then build and launch your customized model:

ollama create qwen-coder-64k -f Modelfile
claude --model qwen-coder-64k

Alternatively, when using cloud models, Ollama manages the expanded context window automatically.

docs.title: 3. Supported Features & Nuances
docs.text: Feature Local Ollama Ollama Cloud Notes File edits ✅ ✅ Models must accurately produce diffs or replacements Bash execution ✅ ✅ Standard permission prompts apply Subagents ✅ ✅ Launches subagent workers with independent context Thinking ✅ ✅ Supported on thinking-compatible models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1) Vision ✅ ✅ Works with multimodal models (e.g. Llama 3.2 Vision) Hosted WebSearch ⚠️ ✅ Ollama Cloud supports native web search; local requires Ollama web search API

docs.title: Hardware Sizing Guide (Mac & PC)
docs.text:
Running coding models with 64k+ context requires understanding your hardware's VRAM limits:

flowchart TD
    Mac[Mac with 16 GB Unified Memory]
    Mac -->|8B Model e.g. Qwen 8B| Safe["✅ Allocates ~11 GB VRAM<br/>Smooth local performance"]
    Mac -->|20B / 32B Model| Swapping["⚠️ Needs 25 GB+ VRAM<br/>Triggers heavy disk swap"]
    Mac -->|Cloud Model :cloud| CloudOpt["⚡ Offloads to Cloud<br/>0 GB local VRAM consumed"]

    style Safe fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#43a047
    style Swapping fill:#ffebee,stroke:#e53935
    style CloudOpt fill:#e0f7fa,stroke:#00838f
Machine / VRAM Recommended Local Model Notes 16 GB Mac (M1/M2/M3/M4) Qwen 2.5 Coder 8B or Gemma 9B Uses ~11 GB VRAM; leaves ~5 GB for macOS and your IDE. Perfect local sweet spot. 24 GB – 36 GB Mac / PC Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B Higher reasoning accuracy, handles multi-file edits with ease. 48 GB – 64 GB Mac Qwen 32B or GPT-OSS 20B Near-frontier local coding accuracy with full 64k+ context. 128 GB+ / Dual GPU Llama 3.3 70B Enterprise-grade local offline development.

docs.title: The Cloud Model Alternative: Free Quotas Without Local VRAM
docs.text:
If your local Mac has 16 GB or less and you hit accuracy limits with 8B models: - Choose cloud-hosted open models (ollama launch claude --model glm-4.7:cloud or kimi-k2.7-code:cloud). - Token Quota: Cloud tiers often include generous allowances (e.g. GLM Cloud provides ~250,000 input tokens per hour free). Since a full Claude Code conversation context is 200,000 tokens, this covers roughly one entire deep coding session every hour completely free.

➡️ Next: Headless automation & /loop

docs.title: 3. Headless Automation & Scheduled Loops
docs.text: Ollama adds two powerful capabilities for automated and recurring development workflows: non-interactive execution (--yes) and scheduled in-session prompts (/loop).

docs.title: 1. Running Headless (CI/CD & Scripts)
docs.text:
When running Claude Code in Docker containers, shell scripts, or CI pipelines, you cannot have interactive terminal prompts asking to select models or confirm model downloads.

Use the --yes flag with ollama launch:

ollama launch claude --model gemma4:cloud --yes -- -p "how does this repository work?"

flowchart LR
    CMD["ollama launch claude"] --> F1["--model gemma4:cloud<br/>(Specifies target model)"]
    CMD --> F2["--yes<br/>(Skips interactive selectors & auto-pulls)"]
    CMD --> SEP["--<br/>(Separator)"]
    SEP --> CC["-p 'how does this repo work?'<br/>(Direct Claude Code CLI flags)"]

docs.title: How --yes Works
docs.text:
1. Requires --model: You must explicitly declare the model.
  2. Auto-pulls missing models: If the local or cloud model is not yet cached, Ollama pulls it automatically without interactive confirmation.
  3. Passes arguments after -- directly to Claude Code: Flags like -p (execute one prompt and exit), --dangerously-skip-permissions (for sandboxed CI), or --output-format are forwarded to the Claude engine.

docs.title: Example: Automated PR Review in a GitHub Action
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ai-review.yml
name: Local AI Code Review
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run automated review with Ollama
        run: |
          ollama launch claude --model qwen2.5-coder:14b --yes -- \
            -p "Review git diff origin/main...HEAD against conventions in CLAUDE.md. List potential bugs."

docs.title: 2. Scheduled In-Session Tasks with /loop
docs.text:
Inside a Claude Code session backed by Ollama, you can run prompts or slash commands automatically at recurring intervals using /loop:

/loop <interval> <prompt or /command>

Supported intervals include minutes (m) and hours (h).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Triage PRs every 30 minutes: 

/loop 30m Check my open PRs and summarize their status

Monitor GitHub issues every 15 minutes: 

/loop 15m Check for new GitHub issues, verify reproduction steps, and triage by priority

Keep up with industry updates every hour: 

/loop 1h Research the latest AI news and summarize key developments

docs.title: /loop vs. Module 04 Routines
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Loop["🔄 /loop (Ollama Integration)"]
        L1["Runs inside the current session"]
        L2["Preserves ongoing conversational context"]
        L3["Great for active monitoring while coding"]
    end

    subgraph Routines["⏰ Module 04 Routines (Claude Desktop)"]
        R1["Launches a fresh session for each run"]
        R2["Operates independently in background / cloud"]
        R3["Great for daily standup / weekly scheduled reports"]
    end

docs.title: 3. Autonomous Permission Management
docs.text:
When running unattended loops or headless scripts, prompts requesting bash or file edit approval would stall execution.

You have two choices:

  1. Granular Rules in settings.json (Recommended): Explicitly pre-approve safe commands in .claude/settings.json: 
    {
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git status)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(pytest *)",
      "Edit(reports/**)"
    ]
  }
}
  2. Bypass Permissions in Sandboxes: In disposable containers or isolated virtual machines only: 
    ollama launch claude --model gemma4:cloud --yes -- --dangerously-skip-permissions -p "Run test suite and fix failing tests"

➡️ Next: Cloud models & channels

docs.title: 4. Cloud Models & Channels
docs.text: You do not need a beefy GPU or even a local Ollama daemon to use Ollama with Claude Code. You can connect directly to Ollama Cloud for serverless inference, leverage web search, or control your Claude Code session over Telegram.

docs.title: 1. Connecting Directly to Ollama Cloud
docs.text:
With an Ollama API key, you can run Claude Code against high-performance cloud-hosted open models (like glm-5.3-flash or kimi-k2.7-code:cloud) without installing the Ollama daemon locally.

flowchart LR
    Dev["Developer Terminal<br/>(Claude Code)"] -->|"HTTPS / v1/messages<br/>Bearer OLLAMA_API_KEY"| Cloud["🌐 Ollama Cloud<br/>(https://ollama.com)"]
    Cloud --> Models["GLM-5.3-flash<br/>Kimi-k2.7<br/>Gemma-4"]

    style Cloud fill:#e0f7fa,stroke:#00838f
    style Dev fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#1e88e5

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Obtain an API key from your Ollama account.
  2. Export your key and point Claude Code's base URL to https://ollama.com:
export OLLAMA_API_KEY="your-api-key-here"

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://ollama.com \
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$OLLAMA_API_KEY" \
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" \
claude --model glm-5.3-flash

Authentication note: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN carries the bearer token header. Always ensure ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" so the client does not try to authenticate against Anthropic's endpoints.

Check the live connection inside Claude Code: 

/status

docs.title: 2. Web Search & Web Fetch
docs.text:
When paired with Ollama, Claude Code can access Ollama's web search API to retrieve live information and documentation.

sequenceDiagram
    participant You
    participant CC as Claude Code
    participant OL as Ollama Web API
    participant Web as Internet

    You->>CC: "What are the latest changes in React 19.2?"
    CC->>OL: Search request
    OL->>Web: Fetch & rank results
    OL-->>CC: Clean markdown summary & citations
    CC-->>You: Synthesized answer

This lets local models query current documentation without hallucinating obsolete package APIs.

docs.title: 3. Remote Control via Telegram Bot
docs.text:
You can connect a Telegram bot to your Claude Code session, allowing you to ask questions, review code, or trigger tasks from your phone while away from your desk.

flowchart LR
    Phone["📱 You on Telegram<br/>(Mobile / Desktop)"] <--> Bot["🤖 Telegram Bot<br/>(@BotFather)"]
    Bot <--> Plugin["🔌 Telegram Plugin<br/>(claude-plugins-official)"]
    Plugin <--> Session["💻 Claude Code Session<br/>(ollama launch claude)"]

    style Phone fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1976d2
    style Session fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#388e3c

docs.title: Setting Up the Telegram Channel
docs.text:
1. Create a bot: Open Telegram, message @BotFather, and create a new bot to receive your bot token.
  2. Install the plugin: Add the official Telegram plugin from the Anthropic plugin repository: 
    /plugins install telegram@claude-plugins-official
  3. Launch with the Telegram channel flag: 
    ollama launch claude -- --channels plugin:telegram@claude-plugins-official

docs.title: Handling Permissions for Remote Bots
docs.text: When chatting with Claude Code over Telegram, interactive confirmation prompts in your terminal can block the bot. - In normal development: define explicit pre-approved patterns in .claude/settings.json (e.g. allowing read/test commands). - In an isolated environment (e.g. dedicated VM or container): pass --dangerously-skip-permissions to let the bot operate autonomously.

docs.title: Summary: When to Use Ollama with Claude Code
docs.text:
Scenario Recommendation Proprietary code with strict zero-cloud policies Local Ollama + Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B or Llama 3.3 Offline work (airplanes, train travel, remote areas) Local Ollama + 14B or 32B model with 64k context Saving Anthropic subscription plan usage Ollama Cloud or local models for routine tasks Remote task orchestration from mobile ollama launch claude + Telegram channel plugin Unattended batch scripts / CI pipeline ollama launch claude --yes -- -p "..."

➡️ Next: Local model tactics & Storybook

docs.title: 5. Local Model Tactics: Component Isolation, Wireframes & Screenshot Loops
docs.text:
Open-source 8B–14B models running on a Mac cannot match Claude 3.5 Sonnet or Opus in raw multi-file architectural reasoning. If you prompt an 8B model with "Build the entire full-stack app", it gets overwhelmed by context, mixes up dependencies, and produces subtle UI bugs (like putting button text into a logo).

To get professional, production-grade output from local models, you must adapt your workflow to their strengths.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Bad["❌ The Rookie Trap"]
        B1["'Build the entire app'"] --> B2["Massive context overload"] --> B3["Hallucinated styles & broken imports"]
    end

    subgraph Good["✅ The Local Model Workflow"]
        G1["1. Isolate Component<br/>(Storybook / Template)"] --> G2["2. Plan Mode +<br/>ASCII Wireframe"]
        G2 --> G3["3. Implement Single File"]
        G3 --> G4["4. Screenshot Loop<br/>for Visual Polish"]
    end

    style Bad fill:#ffebee,stroke:#e53935
    style Good fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#43a047

docs.title: 1. The Storybook Strategy: One Component at a Time
docs.text:
Instead of throwing an entire project directory into the prompt, break your user interface into standalone, atomic components using tools like Storybook or dedicated template files.

# Start Storybook for isolated component development
npm run storybook

Why this transforms local model performance: - Zero context bloat: The model only reads the single component file and its CSS/tailwind definition. - Immediate testability: You can see email templates, dialogs, buttons, and tables rendered in isolation. - Lower parameter demand: A 7B or 8B model (like Qwen 2.5 Coder 8B) performs near frontier-level when constrained to a single 150-line file.

docs.title: 2. Plan Mode + Terminal ASCII Wireframes
docs.text:
Before letting a local model write code, use Plan Mode combined with a request for a terminal ASCII wireframe:

/frontend-design

Prompt Pattern: "Based on the current email verification template, I want you to redesign the email to have a cleaner, more minimalistic look. Before you generate any code, switch to Plan Mode and create a terminal ASCII wireframe to show me the layout and visual hierarchy. Thanks."

docs.title: Why the ASCII Wireframe Matters
docs.text:
Local models often make positioning errors on the first pass (e.g. putting verification actions in the header). An ASCII preview lets you catch structural misunderstandings in seconds before code is touched:

+------------------------------------------+
|                 [LOGO]                   |

If the wireframe looks wrong, refine the prompt in the plan before approving file edits.

docs.title: 3. The Visual Screenshot Refinement Loop
docs.text:
Local models are significantly better at iterative corrections than zero-shot perfection. Use Claude Code's image support to create a tight visual feedback loop:

sequenceDiagram
    participant You
    participant Browser as Browser (Storybook)
    participant CC as Claude Code (Local / Cloud)

    You->>Browser: Inspect rendered component
    You->>CC: Paste screenshot + exact delta:
    Note over You,CC: "Icon is shifted left; center it.<br/>Revert background color to gray."
    CC->>CC: Inspect visual screenshot diff
    CC->>Browser: Update CSS / HTML
    Browser-->>You: Verified pixel-perfect fix

docs.title: Prompt Example with Image:
docs.text:
1. Take a screenshot of the rendered component.
  2. In Claude Code, drag the screenshot into the prompt (or reference the image path): 
    Based on this screenshot of the rendered email:
1. The email icon is shifted to the left — center it above the title.
2. Revert the background color to gray (#f5f5f5) to match our brand card.

docs.title: 4. When to Escalate to Cloud Models
docs.text:
When a task exceeds an 8B local model's capability (such as intricate CSS grid alignments or multi-component state management), use ollama launch claude --config to escalate to a high-capacity cloud model:

Task Type Recommended Tier Model Cost Atomic component styling Local 8B Qwen 2.5 Coder 8B / Gemma 9B 100% Free, Offline Bug fixing in single function Local 8B Qwen 2.5 Coder 8B 100% Free, Offline Complex responsive layout Ollama Cloud GLM 4.7 Cloud / Kimi k2.7 Free Tier (~250k tok/hr) Full application architecture Anthropic Cloud Claude 3.7 Sonnet / Opus Pro / Max Plan

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
You don't need an expensive subscription for every coding task. By adopting Component Isolation (Storybook), Terminal Wireframe previews, and Screenshot feedback loops, local 8B models on a 16 GB Mac deliver outstanding results for everyday development.

docs.title: Model Management
docs.text: Command Description Example ollama list List all local and cloud models available on this machine ollama list ollama ps Show models currently loaded into memory/VRAM ollama ps ollama pull <model> Download or update a model from the registry ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b ollama rm <model> Remove a model to free local disk space ollama rm deepseek-r1:1.5b ollama cp <src> <dest> Duplicate or alias an existing model ollama cp qwen2.5-coder:7b my-coder ollama create <name> -f <file> Create a customized model from a Modelfile ollama create coder-64k -f Modelfile

docs.title: Agent Launching (ollama launch)
docs.text:
Ollama can automatically configure and launch supported coding agents:

ollama launch claude                     # Interactive launch with model picker
ollama launch claude --config            # Configure/switch default model without launching
ollama launch claude --restore           # Reset integration back to default profile
ollama launch claude --model <model>     # Launch directly with target model
ollama launch claude --yes -- -p "..."   # Non-interactive headless prompt (CI/CD)

Other supported integrations: chatgpt, openclaw, opencode, hermes, cline, vscode.

docs.title: Direct Interactive Terminal Chat (ollama run)
docs.text:
To talk directly to a model without agentic coding features:

ollama run gpt-oss:20b-cloud

In-Session Shortcut Commands: - /? or /? shortcuts: Show in-session help. - /bye or Ctrl + D: Exit the session. - """: Begin multi-line input (type """ again on a new line to send). - /set verbose: Print token generation speed (tokens/second) and evaluation time. - /show info: Display active model architecture and context length.

docs.title: Model Inspection (ollama show)
docs.text:
Inspect the internal prompt templates and parameters:

ollama show gpt-oss:20b-cloud                 # Full model card and license
ollama show gpt-oss:20b-cloud --modelfile     # View exact Modelfile definition
ollama show gpt-oss:20b-cloud --parameters    # View num_ctx, temperature, stop tokens
ollama show gpt-oss:20b-cloud --system        # View baked-in system prompt

docs.title: 2. Server Daemon Configuration & Environment Variables
docs.text:
The Ollama daemon can be customized using environment variables. On macOS, set these with launchctl setenv or run manually before ollama serve:

Variable Default Purpose OLLAMA_HOST 127.0.0.1:11434 Bind address. Set to 0.0.0.0:11434 for LAN access. OLLAMA_ORIGINS — Allowed CORS origins for web applications (e.g. * or http://localhost:3000). OLLAMA_MODELS ~/.ollama/models Custom directory path for storing model weights (e.g. external SSD). OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL 1 Number of simultaneous requests a model can handle. OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE 5m Duration to keep idle models in VRAM before unloading (e.g. 1h or -1 for forever). OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION 0 Set to 1 to enable Flash Attention on supported GPUs for faster inference.

docs.title: 3. Python SDK Quickstart (pip install ollama)
docs.text: The official Python library provides native async/sync support, streaming, and function calling.

docs.title: Basic Chat & Streaming
docs.text:
import ollama

# Simple completion
response = ollama.chat(
    model='gpt-oss:20b-cloud',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is the purpose of CLAUDE.md?'}]
)
print(response['message']['content'])

# Real-time streaming
stream = ollama.chat(
    model='gpt-oss:20b-cloud',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Write a Python binary search.'}],
    stream=True,
)
for chunk in stream:
    print(chunk['message']['content'], end='', flush=True)

docs.title: Native Tool Calling with Python Functions
docs.text:
import ollama

def get_current_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the weather for a given city."""
    return f"The weather in {city} is sunny and 21°C."

response = ollama.chat(
    model='gpt-oss:20b-cloud',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is the weather in Berlin?'}],
    tools=[get_current_weather]
)

# Ollama returns structured tool calls
if response['message'].get('tool_calls'):
    for tool in response['message']['tool_calls']:
        print(f"Tool requested: {tool['function']['name']}")
        print(f"Arguments: {tool['function']['arguments']}")

docs.title: Using Anthropic's Official Python SDK with Ollama
docs.text:
Because Ollama provides an Anthropic-compatible API, you can use anthropic-sdk with zero Anthropic subscription:

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(
    base_url="http://localhost:11434",
    api_key="ollama",  # dummy token required by client
)

message = client.messages.create(
    model="gpt-oss:20b-cloud",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain worktrees in Git."}]
)
print(message.content[0].text)
