docs.title: 1. The Core Variable Pattern
docs.text:
Whenever Claude Code starts, it checks your environment (or your local .env file) for three variables:

# 1. The target server endpoint
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="<gateway-or-provider-url>"

# 2. Your authentication token (Bearer token)
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="<your-provider-api-key>"

# 3. Empty out the official key so Claude doesn't ping Anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""

# 4. Launch with the target provider's model ID
claude --model "<provider-model-id>"

docs.title: Provider 1: OpenRouter (Universal Aggregator)
docs.text:
OpenRouter exposes a unified Anthropic-compatible API endpoint. With a single OpenRouter API key, you can run DeepSeek, Meta Llama, Mistral, or Qwen through Claude Code.

In .env: 

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api"
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="sk-or-v1-your-openrouter-key"
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
CLAUDE_OLLAMA_MODEL="deepseek/deepseek-chat"

Launch: 

./launch-claude-ollama.sh deepseek/deepseek-chat

Popular OpenRouter model IDs for coding: - deepseek/deepseek-chat (DeepSeek-V3) - meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct - qwen/qwen-2.5-coder-32b-instruct

docs.title: Provider 2: Ollama Cloud (Serverless without Local Daemon)
docs.text:
If you don't want to run a local daemon on your Mac, connect directly to Ollama's managed infrastructure:

In .env: 

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://ollama.com"
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="your-ollama-api-key"
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
CLAUDE_OLLAMA_MODEL="glm-5.3-flash"

Launch: 

./launch-claude-ollama.sh glm-5.3-flash

docs.title: Provider 3: LiteLLM Proxy (Any LLM in the World)
docs.text:
LiteLLM is an open-source proxy that translates OpenAI, Groq, Cohere, Bedrock, and Azure into the Anthropic Messages format.

  1. Install and start LiteLLM: 
    pip install litellm
litellm --model groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile --port 4000
  2. In .env: 
    ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:4000"
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="sk-litellm-any-key"
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
CLAUDE_OLLAMA_MODEL="groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile"
  3. Launch: 
    ./launch-claude-ollama.sh groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile

docs.title: Provider 4: Cloudflare AI Gateway & Enterprise Proxies
docs.text:
For teams that need centralized audit logs, response caching, rate limits, and spend analytics:

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/{account_id}/{gateway_name}/anthropic"
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="your-custom-gateway-token"
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
CLAUDE_OLLAMA_MODEL="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"

docs.title: 3. The 2 Mandatory Requirements for Any Provider
docs.text:
Not every model or provider endpoint works automatically with Claude Code. Verify that the provider satisfies these two rules:

Requirement Why it's required What happens if missing Anthropic Messages Schema (/v1/messages) Claude Code sends structured payloads expecting streaming Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream). HTTP 404 or payload parsing error. Tool / Function Calling Support Claude Code is an agent that reads files (View), edits code (Edit), and runs bash (Bash). The model will reply with text descriptions instead of executing real actions.

docs.title: 4. Security & Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep Secrets in .env: Never hardcode API keys in settings.json or committed scripts.
  2. Verify .gitignore: Ensure .env is listed in your project's .gitignore so tokens are never pushed to GitHub.
  3. Check Connection Status: Whenever you change providers, run /status inside Claude Code to verify that the active URL and model match your target endpoint.
> /status
Model: deepseek/deepseek-chat
API Base URL: https://openrouter.ai/api
Context Window: 200,000 tokens

✅ Module complete. Continue with Lab 10 — Ollama & Local Models.

docs.title: Module 08 — NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Agentic Platform
docs.text:
Goal: Turn an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor (Blackwell architecture, 128 GB Unified Memory) into a local, high-throughput AI inference and autonomous agentic engineering platform while preserving development safety on your Mac.

# Lesson / Chapter Time 1 Target Architecture & Hybrid Topology 15 min 2 9-Phase Roadmap & Release Gates (M0–M8) 20 min 3 Hardware Audit & Secure Infrastructure (M0–M1) 15 min 4 Local Inference: Ollama, vLLM & Prefix Caching (M2 & M5) 25 min 5 Agentic Coding MVP & Benchmarking (M3–M4) 20 min 6 Autonomous Execution & Git Worktree Isolation (M6) 20 min 7 Engineering Adapters: STM32, KiCad & ROS 2 (M7) 25 min 8 Operations, Monitoring & Implementation Brief (M8) 15 min

docs.title: Executive Overview
docs.text:
The NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor represents a generational leap for local and edge AI engineering. Powered by NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU architecture, unified LPDDR5X memory (128 GB), and advanced tensor cores supporting native FP4 and FP8 precision, Thor can host 30B to 80B parameter coding models entirely locally without relying on external cloud APIs.

flowchart LR
    Mac["💻 Mac (Developer Host)<br/>VS Code · OpenCode · Claude Code<br/>Git Repositories · Local Tools"]

    Tunnel["🔒 Encrypted SSH Tunnel<br/>Port 11434 / 11500"]

    Thor["🚀 NVIDIA AGX Thor (AI Compute Node)<br/>128 GB Unified Memory · Blackwell GPU<br/>Ollama / vLLM · Model Gateway"]

    Mac <-->|Private LAN / Zero-Trust| Tunnel
    Tunnel <--> Thor

    classDef mac fill:#1e293b,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef tunnel fill:#0284c7,stroke:#0369a1,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef thor fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px;

    class Mac mac;
    class Tunnel tunnel;
    class Thor thor;

docs.title: Why a Hybrid Architecture?
docs.text:
Running both heavy LLM inference and resource-intensive build pipelines (such as CMake, Ninja, GCC, and ROS 2 builds) on a single embedded device can overwhelm unified memory and trigger the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer.

By adopting a hybrid topology: - Your Mac acts as the primary developer interface, hosting the IDE, local Git repositories, and tool execution. - AGX Thor acts as an uncompromised, high-speed neural compute node, serving models via Ollama or vLLM over a zero-trust SSH tunnel. - Isolated Containers (running on Mac or Thor) execute automated builds and tests inside isolated Git worktrees.

docs.text:
gantt

docs.title: Key Invariants & Safety Principles
docs.text:
1. Inference and Execution Are Separated: The LLM does not get an unrestricted host shell. All actions flow through structured tool adapters.
  2. Fail-Closed Safety Gates: Destructive operations (hardware flashing, PCB fabrication release, Git branch pushes) require explicit human approval.
  3. Task Isolation via Git Worktrees: Every task executes in an ephemeral Git worktree (git worktree add ../task-xxx), keeping the main branch untouched until review.
  4. Interchangeable Inferenz-Backends: Start with Ollama for zero-friction setup; transition to vLLM with Prefix Caching for 5x–10x multi-turn agent acceleration.
  5. Measurable Verification: An agent cannot pass its own task simply by declaring success; passing unit tests and clean linter outputs are non-negotiable.

docs.title: Target Architecture & Hybrid Topology
docs.text: Building a reliable, local-first agentic coding platform requires clear separation between user interaction, model inference, and tool execution.

docs.title: 1. System Topology Overview

docs.title: 1. Separate Inference from Execution
docs.text: The LLM compute server must remain responsive and resilient. It does not provide an unrestricted shell directly to the model. - Inference Server: Performs token generation and returns structured tool-call arguments. - Agent Runtime: Evaluates tool calls, enforces permission boundaries, executes actions in isolated environments, and feeds back structured outputs.

docs.title: 2. Task Isolation via Git Worktrees
docs.text:
No agent writes directly to active feature or main branches. Every task is given an isolated Git worktree: 

git worktree add ../task-feature-x -b agent/task-feature-x
This isolates concurrent edits, prevents broken build environments from polluting the repository, and makes rollback instantaneous.

docs.title: 3. Interchangeable Model Engines
docs.text: The architecture couples to standard APIs (Anthropic Messages API and OpenAI /v1 format), not specific vendor binaries. - Transitioning from Ollama to vLLM requires updating the backend port or URL without altering agent prompts or project code.

docs.title: 4. Measurable and Verifiable Diffs
docs.text: Every proposed modification must exist as a standard Git diff. Success is measured by concrete execution results: - Does the code compile? - Do regression tests pass (pytest, colcon test, ctest)? - Does the static analysis report zero new violations?

docs.title: 5. Fail-Closed Boundaries for Hardware and Production
docs.text: No automated system should possess permissions to: - Push to protected branches (main, release/*). - Flash connected microcontrollers (st-flash, openocd). - Release PCB Gerber or drill files for manufacturing. These operations must remain gated behind explicit human operator authorization.

docs.title: 3. Resource Partitioning on AGX Thor (128 GB Unified Memory)
docs.text:
Because the AGX Thor uses unified LPDDR5X memory shared between CPU and GPU, careful budgeting is required to prevent Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) aborts:

Memory Component Allocation Role & Usage Notes JetPack 7.x OS & System Services ~4 GB Linux kernel, systemd, SSH, Docker daemon Model Weights (Qwen3-Coder 30B MoE Q4) ~19 GB Active working model for day-to-day coding Model Weights (Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B Q4) ~52 GB High-capacity model for complex refactoring PagedAttention KV-Cache (64k context) ~16–28 GB Context retention across multi-turn agent sessions Reserved Operational Headroom ~35–45 GB Build processes, compiler invocations, I/O buffers

[!IMPORTANT] Never let compiler toolchains (e.g., parallel ninja or colcon builds) run on Thor without strict cgroup memory caps (docker run --memory 16g) when an 80B model is loaded.

docs.title: 9-Phase Roadmap & Release Gates (M0–M8)
docs.text: This roadmap outlines the complete path from initial hardware discovery to an autonomous, multi-domain AI engineering platform.

docs.title: 1. Roadmap Overview & Timeline
docs.text:
The platform is designed in progressive phases. Phase M3 delivers the first fully functional MVP; later milestones expand throughput, autonomy, and domain coverage.

Milestone Title Focus & Deliverable Effort Priority M0 Hardware & System Audit Inventory Thor, JetPack, CUDA, GPU detection, baseline report 0.5–1 Day P0 M1 Secure Infrastructure Persistent storage /srv/agentic/, Docker runtime, SSH isolation 1–2 Days P0 M2 Local LLM Inference Ollama container, Qwen3-Coder 30B, GPU validation, API check 1–2 Days P0 M3 Agentic Coding MVP SSH tunnel, OpenCode / Claude Code connection, 6 MVP tests 1–3 Days P0 M4 Model Benchmarking 20-task benchmark suite, 30B vs 80B, TTFT, tool-call accuracy 2–3 Days P1 M5 Optimized Inference (vLLM) vLLM container, Prefix Caching, FP8/NVFP4, KV-cache tuning 2–4 Days P1 M6 Autonomous Execution Git worktree lifecycle, container isolation, step limits 2–4 Days P1 M7 Engineering Adapters Python, STM32 firmware, KiCad ERC/DRC, ROS 2 containers 2–4 Days P1 M8 Monitoring & Operations Observability, health checks, automated recovery, disaster drills 1–3 Days P1

docs.text:
A subsequent gate never replaces a prior gate. If an optimization in M5 regresses tool-call accuracy established in M3, the configuration is rejected.

    G0["Gate M0: Hardware Audited & GPU Detected"] --> G1["Gate M1: Storage Persistent & SSH Secured"]
    G1 --> G2["Gate M2: Model Loaded, GPU Verified, API Healthy"]
    G2 --> G3["Gate M3: End-to-End Bugfix & Test Passed"]

docs.title: Milestone Acceptance Checklist
docs.text:
• M0: Hardware variant, JetPack 7.x, CUDA version, and storage verified.
  • M1: Container runtime operational, NVMe storage isolated, SSH key auth enforced.
  • M2: Ollama running locally on Thor; GPU utilization confirmed during token decode.
  • M3: Agent on Mac autonomously diagnoses a bug, implements a fix, runs pytest, and outputs a clean git diff.
  • M4: Structured benchmark report completed comparing throughput, TTFT, and tool-call schema accuracy.
  • M5: vLLM deployed with prefix caching; measured latency improvement on multi-turn prompts.
  • M6: Automated task orchestration inside ephemeral Git worktrees with strict timeout and retry guards.
  • M7: Automated firmware compilation (STM32), KiCad ERC/DRC validation, and ROS 2 build verified.
  • M8: Clean recovery after cold reboot; service status monitored via structured telemetry.

docs.title: 3. Risk Matrix & Mitigations
docs.text: Identified Risk Impact Architectural Mitigation Strategy Thor / JetPack Container Drift Blocker Pin exact Docker container digests; verify JetPack 7.2.1 / L4T 39.2.1 compatibility before updating. Unified Memory Exhaustion High Keep model weights + KV cache under 80 GB; enforce strict memory limits (--memory) on build containers. Tool-Call Schema Hallucination High Use models fine-tuned on Hermes / Anthropic tool-calling schemas (e.g. Qwen3-Coder); test with strict JSON schema validators. Multi-File Refactoring Corruption Medium Execute all edits in isolated Git worktrees (../task-xxx); reject changes failing regression tests. Infinite Repair / Retry Loops Medium Enforce maximum step limits (e.g., max 15 tool calls per task, max 3 repair attempts per failure). Unauthorized Hardware Flash Critical Place st-flash and openocd behind a fail-closed gate requiring interactive human confirmation. Prompt Injection in Repositories High Treat untrusted source code and issues as passive data; never execute dynamic scripts extracted from unvetted prompt text.

docs.title: Hardware Audit & Secure Infrastructure (M0–M1)
docs.text: Before launching models or running agent containers, establish the baseline truth of the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor hardware and lock down the host infrastructure.

docs.title: 1. Phase M0 — Hardware & System Audit (Priority P0)
docs.text: The goal of M0 is to inspect the system as-is, capturing kernel versions, CUDA support, available storage, and thermal baselines before modifying software.

docs.title: Diagnostic Execution Commands
docs.text:
Run the following inspection commands directly on the AGX Thor terminal:

# 1. Jetson Linux release & architecture
cat /etc/nv_tegra_release
uname -a
uname -m

# 2. GPU detection & driver status
nvidia-smi

# 3. Memory & NVMe storage capacity
free -h
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
df -h

# 4. Docker & NVIDIA Container Runtime validation
docker --version
docker info | grep -i -A 5 runtimes

# 5. Network interfaces & IP addresses
ip -br addr

docs.title: Target Software Stack
docs.text:
NVIDIA's baseline documentation designates JetPack 7.2.1 with Jetson Linux 39.2.1 as the reference release for the AGX Thor.

Target Environment:
- SoC: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor (Blackwell Tensor Cores)
- CPU: ARM64 (aarch64) multi-core high-performance cluster
- Unified Memory: 128 GB LPDDR5X
- OS: Jetson Linux 39.2.1 (based on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / JetPack 7.2.1)
- CUDA: 12.8+ / Compute Capability 10.x (Blackwell)

docs.title: Deliverables for Phase M0
docs.text:
1. hardware_inventory.md: Complete hardware inventory and serials.
  2. system_audit.json: Machine-readable dump of nvidia-smi --query-gpu, lscpu, and lsblk.
  3. baseline_report.md: Idle power consumption, baseline thermal readings, and free storage margin.

docs.title: 2. Phase M1 — Secure Infrastructure Setup (Priority P0)
docs.text: Establish the AGX Thor as a hardened, reproducible AI compute server.

docs.title: 2.1 Persistent Storage Partitioning
docs.text:
All AI-related assets are separated from the root OS filesystem and mounted under /srv/agentic/:

/srv/agentic/
├── config/             # Model, agent, and security policies (.yaml)
├── models/             # Weights survive container restarts
│   ├── ollama/         # GGUF model blobs
│   └── huggingface/    # Checkpoints for vLLM (Safetensors)
├── cache/              # KV-cache and prompt prefix caches
├── containers/         # Isolated Docker build contexts
├── logs/               # Structured inference and audit logs
├── benchmarks/         # Benchmark datasets and performance traces
├── backups/            # Configuration snapshots and task states
└── artifacts/          # Generated diffs, test logs, and reports

Create the directory structure with appropriate ownership: 

sudo mkdir -p /srv/agentic/{config,models/ollama,models/huggingface,cache,containers,logs,benchmarks,backups,artifacts}
sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /srv/agentic
chmod -R 750 /srv/agentic

docs.title: 2.2 Docker & NVIDIA Container Runtime
docs.text:
Verify that the NVIDIA Container Runtime is configured as the default runtime for Docker:

docker info --format '{{json .Runtimes}}'

If nvidia is missing, configure /etc/docker/daemon.json: 

{
  "runtimes": {
    "nvidia": {
      "path": "nvidia-container-runtime",
      "runtimeArgs": []
    }
  },
  "default-runtime": "nvidia"
}
Restart Docker: 
sudo systemctl restart docker

[!WARNING] Thor uses the Blackwell GPU architecture. Do not pull generic linux/arm64 containers built for Jetson Orin (Ampere architecture). Always use container images tagged specifically for JetPack 7 / Thor.

docs.title: 2.3 Network Hardening & Zero-Trust Access
docs.text:
Apply strict firewall rules to prevent unauthenticated access: 1. Public Exposure: Zero open ports to the WAN. 2. Inference Port: Ollama (11434) and vLLM (8000) bind strictly to 127.0.0.1. 3. SSH Access: Enforce ED25519 public-key authentication; disable password authentication and root login: 

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardened.conf
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
X11Forwarding no
4. Remote Access from Mac: All connections traverse an SSH tunnel or a private Tailscale mesh.

docs.title: Local Inference: Ollama, vLLM & Prefix Caching (M2 & M5)
docs.text: Inference on AGX Thor evolves in two stages: Ollama for immediate, stable validation (M2), followed by vLLM with Prefix Caching and FP8/NVFP4 for maximum multi-turn agent throughput (M5).

docs.title: 1. Phase M2 — Local Inference with Ollama (Priority P0)
docs.text: Ollama provides the fastest path to verified GPU inference without complex engine builds.

docs.title: 1.1 Running the Ollama Jetson Container
docs.text:
Start Ollama with persistent storage mapped to /srv/agentic/models/ollama:

docker run -d \
  --name ollama-thor \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --runtime nvidia \
  --gpus all \
  --network host \
  -v /srv/agentic/models/ollama:/root/.ollama \
  -e OLLAMA_HOST="127.0.0.1:11434" \
  ollama/ollama:latest

docs.title: 1.2 Pulling the Primary Coding Model
docs.text:
Download Qwen3-Coder 30B (Q4_K_M, ~19 GB on disk): 

ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b

[!NOTE] Qwen3-Coder 30B is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture activating approximately 3.3 billion parameters per token. This provides the code comprehension of a much larger model with the generation speed of a small dense network.

docs.title: 1.3 Verifying Real GPU Execution
docs.text:
Never assume a passing command implies GPU execution. Verify during generation:

# In terminal A: trigger a test inference
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3-coder:30b",
    "prompt": "Write a Python function implementing an LRU cache with threading locks.",
    "stream": false
  }' | jq .response

# In terminal B: verify GPU offload and VRAM allocation
ollama ps
nvidia-smi

ollama ps must report 100% GPU offload and nvidia-smi must show the model resident in Unified Memory.

docs.title: 1.4 Model Catalog
docs.text: Model Variant Size (VRAM) Primary Role Phase Qwen3-Coder 30B Q4_K_M (MoE) ~19 GB Daily coding, fast tool execution, unit tests M2 (P0) Qwen3.6 27B Q4_K_M / FP8 ~17 GB Code review, architectural analysis, reasoning M2 (P1) Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B Q4_K_M ~52 GB Deep multi-file refactoring, large migrations M4 (P1) Qwen2.5-Coder 7B Q4_K_M ~4.7 GB Fast router, classifier, intent extraction M2 (P2)

docs.title: 1.5 Context Sizing Strategy
docs.text:
Do not jump straight to 256k tokens. Context consumption scales quadratically with attention mechanisms unless carefully budgeted:

flowchart LR
    A["16K Tokens<br/>Smoke Test & Basic Files"] --> B["32K Tokens<br/>Standard Coding & Multi-file"]
    B --> C["64K Tokens<br/>Target Agent Profile (OpenCode / Claude Code)"]

docs.title: 2. Phase M5 — Inference Optimization with vLLM (Priority P1)
docs.text: While Ollama is simple to operate, multi-turn coding agents generate huge repetitive prompts (resending the system prompt, project context, and history on every turn). vLLM's Prefix Caching turns this into an order-of-magnitude acceleration.

docs.title: 2.1 Why Prefix Caching Is Essential for Agents
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Agent as Coding Agent
    participant Engine as vLLM / Thor

    Note over Agent, Engine: Turn 1: 25,000 Tokens (System Prompt + Repo Index)
    Agent->>Engine: Send Initial Task
    Engine->>Engine: Compute Prefill on 25k tokens (~2.5s)
    Engine-->>Agent: Output: "I will read src/api.py"

    Note over Agent, Engine: Turn 2: 26,200 Tokens (History + New Tool Call)
    Agent->>Engine: Read Output returned
    alt Without Prefix Caching
        Engine->>Engine: Re-computes Prefill on entire 26,200 tokens (~2.6s)
    else With vLLM Prefix Caching (--enable-prefix-caching)
        Engine->>Engine: Cache HIT on first 25k tokens (0.02s)! Only prefill 1.2k tokens.
    end
    Engine-->>Agent: Output: "Generating patch..."

docs.title: 2.2 Optimization Matrix on Blackwell
docs.text: Optimization Technique Expected Benefit Thor Hardware Prerequisite Prefix Caching Reduces multi-turn prompt prefill latency by 80–95% vLLM --enable-prefix-caching NVFP4 Precision 2x inference throughput over FP8 on Blackwell Tensor Cores Quantized NVFP4 checkpoint FP8 KV-Cache Cuts KV-cache RAM usage by 50% at 64k context --kv-cache-dtype fp8 Continuous Batching Parallel agent worker requests without queue blocking vLLM PagedAttention

docs.title: 2.3 Deploying the vLLM Jetson Thor Container
docs.text:
Launch the official NVIDIA Jetson Thor vLLM container:

docker run -d \
  --name vllm-thor \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --runtime nvidia \
  --gpus all \
  --network host \
  --ipc host \
  -v /srv/agentic/models/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  ghcr.io/nvidia-ai-iot/vllm:latest-jetson-thor \
  --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 11500 \
  --max-model-len 65536 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.75

docs.title: 2.4 Acceptance Criteria for M5
docs.text: vLLM is promoted to production only if: 1. Tool-call schema compliance matches or exceeds the Ollama baseline. 2. Multi-turn time-to-first-token (TTFT) drops by at least 50%. 3. Memory consumption remains stable under a sustained 64k token context window.

docs.title: Agentic Coding MVP & Benchmarking (M3–M4)
docs.text: With local inference verified on AGX Thor, connect your Mac development environment to execute the Agentic Coding MVP (M3) and establish a Systematic Benchmarking Suite (M4).

docs.title: 1. Phase M3 — Agentic Coding MVP on the Mac (Priority P0)
docs.text: The MVP goal is simple: an AI agent running on your Mac uses Thor as its brain to autonomously diagnose a bug, write a patch, run tests, and output a clean Git diff.

docs.title: 1.1 Encrypted Tunneling
docs.text:
On your Mac, establish a background SSH tunnel forwarding local port 11500 to Thor's internal Ollama/vLLM port:

ssh -N -f -L 11500:127.0.0.1:11434 cc@thor-agx.local

Verify connectivity from your Mac: 

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11500/v1/models | jq .

docs.title: 1.2 Connecting OpenCode v2
docs.text:
OpenCode v2 natively supports local Ollama endpoints. Create ~/.config/opencode/config.json:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "ollama/qwen3-coder:30b",
  "providers": {
    "ollama": {
      "settings": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:11500/v1"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 1.3 Connecting Claude Code
docs.text:
Because Claude Code uses the Anthropic Messages API, point it to the Ollama endpoint:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11500
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
claude

docs.title: 2. Progressive Permission Tiers
docs.text:
Do not grant an agent unrestricted write or terminal privileges on day one. Progress through 4 authorization levels:

flowchart TD
    T1["Tier 1: Read-Only<br/>Inspect repo, search files, read docs"] --> T2["Tier 2: Workspace Write<br/>Modify files only inside ephemeral worktree"]
    T2 --> T3["Tier 3: Test Execution<br/>Run pytest, linters, compilers with timeouts"]
    T3 --> T4["Tier 4: Controlled Autonomy<br/>Multi-turn task loops, automatic repair cycles"]

    style T1 fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1
    style T2 fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706
    style T3 fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d
    style T4 fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#7e22ce

docs.title: 3. The 6 MVP Acceptance Tests
docs.text:
To validate M3, create a dedicated test repository with intentional bugs and failing assertions. The agent must pass all 6 criteria without manual intervention:

  • 1. Autonomous Analysis: Discovers repository structure, identifies the entry point, and summarizes module boundaries.
  • 2. Bug Localization: Locates a deliberate off-by-one or edge-case bug based solely on a failing test report.
  • 3. Surgical Implementation: Writes a minimal patch modifying only the affected function; adds a regression test.
  • 4. Test Execution & Repair: Executes pytest, detects any remaining failure, adjusts the patch, and re-runs tests until 100% green.
  • 5. Multi-File Refactoring: Propagates a renamed interface or updated type signature across at least three files consistently.
  • 6. Audit & Diff Generation: Generates a standard git diff and a Markdown summary report explaining the rationale.

Outcome of M3: The core agentic coding loop works reliably end-to-end.

docs.title: 4. Phase M4 — Systematic LLM Benchmarking (Priority P1)
docs.text: Do not rely on subjective impressions. Build an automated benchmark runner to evaluate model variants (e.g. Qwen3-Coder 30B vs. Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B vs. Qwen3.6 27B) across concrete metrics.

docs.title: 4.1 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
docs.text: Metric Measurement Unit Operational Impact TTFT (Time-to-First-Token) Seconds Interactive responsiveness during live sessions Decode Speed Tokens / second Completion velocity for code generation Prefill Speed Tokens / second Ability to digest large repositories & multi-file context Memory Peak GB Unified Memory Headroom margin under 128 GB ceiling Cache Hit Rate % tokens reused Efficiency of agent multi-turn conversation loops Tool Call Success Rate % valid JSON arguments Elimination of malformed tool-call retries Task Completion Rate % passed unit tests Real-world problem-solving capability

docs.title: 4.2 The 20-Task Benchmark Suite
docs.text:
Structure 20 reproducible test cases across 6 engineering categories:

Domain Test Count Evaluation Rubric Python 4 tasks Algorithm bugfix, asyncio race condition, CLI parser, typed model refactor C/C++ 4 tasks Memory leak fix (valgrind), CMake target linking, pointer bounds, header isolation Embedded STM32 3 tasks HAL GPIO initialization, DMA buffer alignment, peripheral state machine Repository Refactor 3 tasks Deprecate class across 5 files, split monolithic module into hexagonal layers Tool Calling Reliability 3 tasks Complex nested JSON arguments, multi-tool parallel calls, handling tool errors Architecture Analysis 3 tasks Generating Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), finding circular imports

docs.title: 4.3 Model Decision Gate
docs.text: Before a model is promoted to the default coding engine on Thor, it must satisfy: 1. Tool-Call Compliance: $\ge 90\%$ valid JSON schema calls. 2. Task Completion: $\ge 80\%$ green test results on simple and intermediate tasks. 3. Stability: Zero out-of-memory aborts during a sustained 64k token session.

docs.title: Autonomous Execution & Git Worktree Isolation (M6)
docs.text: In Phase M6, the platform evolves from interactive human-guided coding to controlled, autonomous task execution.

docs.title: 1. Specialist Agent Topology
docs.text:
You do not need five separate 80B models running in parallel. Instead, use a single high-performance model on AGX Thor that adopts distinct system prompts and permissions based on the role:

flowchart TD
    Task["Incoming Task (Jira / GitHub Issue / CLI Prompt)"] --> Orch["Task Orchestrator<br/>State Machine · Timeouts · Budgeting"]

    Orch --> Planner["Planning Agent<br/>System Prompt: Architecture & Task Breakdown"]
    Planner --> PlanArtifact["Implementation Plan (Plan.md)"]

    PlanArtifact --> Coder["Coding Agent<br/>System Prompt: Surgical Code Edits in Worktree"]
    Coder --> ValRunner["Validation Runner (Deterministic)<br/>Runs pytest / ruff / cmake (No LLM required!)"]

    ValRunner -->|Tests Failed| RepairLoop{"Repair Count < 3?"}
    RepairLoop -->|Yes| Coder
    RepairLoop -->|No| FailedState["Mark Task FAILED<br/>Generate Failure Diagnostic"]

    ValRunner -->|Tests Green| Reviewer["Review Agent<br/>System Prompt: Security & Style Audit"]

    Reviewer --> Gate["Human Quality Gate<br/>Interactive Sign-off on Generated Diff"]
    Gate -->|Approved| Merge["Merge Worktree to Feature Branch"]

docs.title: 2. The Agent Task Lifecycle
docs.text:
Every task transitions through an explicit state machine with enforced timeout and cancellation rules:

CREATED
   │
   ▼
VALIDATED (Prompt & bounds checked)
   │
   ▼
PLANNED (Steps articulated)
   │
   ▼
IMPLEMENTING (Edits applied to worktree)
   │
   ▼
TESTING ───► FAILED
   │            │
   │            ▼
   │         REPAIR (Max 3 iterations)
   │            │
   ◄────────────┘
   │
   ▼
REVIEW (Architecture & security audit)
   │
   ▼
AWAITING_APPROVAL (Human operator sign-off)
   │
   ▼
COMPLETED

docs.title: 3. Git Worktree Isolation
docs.text:
Never allow an autonomous agent to execute directly in your active development directory. Instead, provision an ephemeral Git worktree for every task:

# 1. Create task-specific branch and isolated working directory
git worktree add ../agent-worktrees/task-104 -b agent/task-104

# 2. Run agent container mounted strictly to that worktree
docker run --rm \
  --name agent-task-104 \
  --network none \
  --memory 16g \
  --cpus 8 \
  -v /srv/agentic/worktrees/task-104:/workspace:rw \
  agent-runner:latest \
  --task-id task-104

# 3. Upon completion, inspect the isolated diff
git -C ../agent-worktrees/task-104 diff main

# 4. Clean up worktree after merge or rejection
git worktree remove ../agent-worktrees/task-104

docs.title: 4. Enforcement of Execution Guardrails
docs.text:
To prevent run-away agent loops or resource starvation, enforce strict limits:

Protective Guardrail Operational Limit Enforcement Mechanism Max Agent Turns 20 tool calls per task Orchestrator step counter Max Repair Attempts 3 attempts per failure category State machine transition guard Tool Execution Timeout 60 seconds per shell command Subprocess kill signal (SIGKILL) Filesystem Boundary Only mounted worktree directory Docker rootless volume mount Network Egress Deny all outbound traffic --network none (or allowlist for package mirrors) Git Push Permission Strictly disabled Git credentials omitted from sandbox Secret Protection .env and API keys masked Pre-execution regex filter Durable Audit Trail All prompts, tool calls, and diffs saved JSONL event recorder in /srv/agentic/artifacts/

docs.title: 5. Hexagonal Modularity for the Platform
docs.text:
When building the platform software (e.g. thor-agentic-dev), maintain strict hexagonal architecture boundaries:

src/
├── core/                   # Pure entities: Task, Plan, Diff, AuditRecord (Zero I/O)
├── ports/                  # Interfaces: ModelGatewayPort, ToolAdapterPort, WorktreePort
├── adapters/               # Implementations:
│   ├── git/                # Git worktree and commit adapter
│   ├── model/              # Ollama / vLLM HTTP client
│   └── shell/              # Subprocess runner with timeout & secret masking
├── application/            # Orchestrator, State Machine, Repair Policy
└── quality/                # Quality Gates, Test Evaluation, Diff Scoring

This ensures that upgrading from Ollama to vLLM, or switching from Docker to firecracker microVMs, requires updating only a single adapter module without touching orchestration logic.

docs.title: Engineering Adapters: STM32, KiCad & ROS 2 (M7)
docs.text: Phase M7 specializes the AGX Thor agentic platform for real-world hardware, firmware, and robotics engineering domains.

docs.title: 1. Engineering Adapter Matrix
docs.text:
Each engineering discipline is encapsulated in a dedicated tool adapter implementing a common interface:

Domain Underlying Toolchain Automated Agent Capabilities Safety Boundary Python pytest, Ruff, mypy Bugfixes, refactoring, test execution, typing enforcement Ephemeral worktree C/C++ CMake, Ninja, Clang-Tidy Cross-compilation, pointer validation, static analysis Subprocess timeout STM32 ARM GCC, CubeMX, OpenOCD Firmware synthesis, register abstraction, build verification No auto-flash KiCad KiCad CLI, Python IPC Automated ERC & DRC checks, BoM diff generation No auto-order ROS 2 colcon, rclpy, rclcpp Package building, node creation, QoS validation Container isolation Documentation MkDocs Material, Mermaid Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), API docs Read/write docs dir

docs.title: 2. KiCad PCB Adapter Architecture
docs.text:
Automating electronic hardware design requires separating headless CLI checks from stateful IPC (Inter-Process Communication) tools:

flowchart LR
    Agent["Coding Agent"] --> KiCadAdapter["KiCad Engineering Adapter"]

    subgraph HeadlessCLI ["Headless CLI Checks (Immediate)"]
        ERC["kicad-cli sch erc --output report.json"]
        DRC["kicad-cli pcb drc --output drc.json"]
        BOM["kicad-cli sch export bom"]
    end

    subgraph StatefulIPC ["KiCad IPC Server (Optional)"]
        IPCServer["KiCad Python API Server (Port 9999)"]
        Routing["Placement & Routing Inspection"]
    end

    KiCadAdapter --> HeadlessCLI
    KiCadAdapter --> StatefulIPC

    HeadlessCLI --> Aggregator["Result Aggregator & Gate"]
    Aggregator -->|DRC Errors > 0| Reject["Block Task (Violations Found)"]
    Aggregator -->|DRC Clean| Report["Generate Engineering PCB Diff"]

docs.title: Capabilities of kicad_adapter:
docs.text:
1. Automated ERC Check: Runs kicad-cli sch erc and parses violations into structured JSON.
  2. Automated DRC Check: Runs kicad-cli pcb drc on the .kicad_pcb layout. Any clearance, trace width, or unrouted net error marks the task FAILED.
  3. Bill of Materials (BoM) Diff: Detects added, removed, or modified components and generates an itemized diff table.
  4. Gerber Generation Gate: Exporting fabrication Gerbers is permitted only upon human operator sign-off.

docs.title: 3. STM32 Embedded Firmware Pipeline
docs.text:
Firmware development on AGX Thor follows a strict verification pipeline where physical flashing is explicitly separated from building:

flowchart TD
    Req["Firmware Feature / Bugfix Task"] --> Impl["Firmware Implementation (C / C++)"]
    Impl --> Build["CMake & ARM GCC Cross-Compilation"]

    Build -->|Compile Error| FixLoop["Agent Auto-Fix (Max 3 retries)"]
    FixLoop --> Impl

    Build -->|Binary Generated| StaticAnalysis["Static Analysis (cppcheck & clang-tidy)"]
    StaticAnalysis --> EmulatedTests["Host Unit Tests (Unity / CppUTest)"]

    EmulatedTests --> Report["Generate Firmware Audit Report<br/>(Flash/RAM size, checksums)"]

    Report --> Gate{"Human Operator Approval"}
    Gate -->|Approved| Flash["Flash Target via ST-Link / OpenOCD"]
    Gate -->|Rejected| Abort["Abort Deployment"]

    style Gate fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:2px;
    style Flash fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,stroke-width:2px;

[!CAUTION] Zero Auto-Flash Rule: The agent sandbox must not have access to USB device nodes (/dev/bus/usb) or debug probes. Flashing microcontrollers without an oscilloscope or current-limited bench power supply risks permanent hardware damage.

docs.title: 4. ROS & ROS 2 Robotics Containers
docs.text:
Robotics projects frequently suffer from library conflicts across ROS distributions. AGX Thor uses dedicated, isolated ARM64 containers:

/srv/agentic/containers/ros/
├── ros2-jazzy/             # Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 + ROS 2 Jazzy
│   └── Dockerfile
└── ros2-iron/              # Ubuntu 22.04 ARM64 + ROS 2 Iron
    └── Dockerfile

docs.title: Architecture Rules for ROS Integration:
docs.text:
1. Never Mix Distributions: ROS 1 (Noetic) and ROS 2 environments must never share Python virtual environments or system paths.
  2. ARM64 Native Packages: Because AGX Thor is an ARM64 system, verify that all external ROS drivers (e.g. LiDAR, depth cameras, CAN transceivers) provide aarch64 binaries or compile from source.
  3. Automated Colcon Testing: 
    colcon build --symlink-install --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
colcon test --event-handlers console_direct+
colcon test-result --verbose
  4. QoS Profile Validation: Agents modifying pub/sub communication must explicitly declare QoS reliability and durability profiles to prevent silent dropped messages.

docs.title: Operations, Monitoring & Implementation Brief (M8)
docs.text: Phase M8 hardens the AGX Thor platform for reliable 24/7 autonomous operation and provides a formal implementation brief to guide future coding agents.

docs.title: 1. Observability & Telemetry Dashboard
docs.text:
A local Python telemetry daemon monitors system health and streams metrics to lightweight logging endpoints:

flowchart LR
    ThorSensors["Hardware Sensors<br/>(tegrastats · sysfs · nvidia-smi)"] --> Collector["Metrics Collector Daemon"]
    InferenceAPI["Ollama / vLLM API"] --> Collector
    AgentRunner["Task Orchestrator"] --> Collector

    Collector --> Dashboard["Monitoring Telemetry<br/>(Structured JSON / Grafana)"]

    subgraph TrackedKPIs ["Critical Operational KPIs"]
        GPU["GPU Utilization (%)"]
        RAM["Unified Memory Used (GB)"]
        Temp["SoC Temperature (°C)"]
        Power["Power Consumption (Watts)"]
        Speed["Tokens/sec & TTFT (s)"]
        TaskRate["Task Success Rate (%)"]
    end

    Dashboard --- TrackedKPIs

docs.title: Telemetry Thresholds
docs.text: Metric Target Normal Warning Threshold Critical Action Unified Memory $\le 85\text{ GB}$ $105\text{ GB}$ Pause new tasks; evict idle KV-caches SoC Temperature $\le 65^\circ\text{C}$ $80^\circ\text{C}$ Ramp active cooling fan to 100% Power Consumption $\le 75\text{ W}$ $110\text{ W}$ Cap parallel batch concurrency Consecutive Task Fails 0 3 failures Lock orchestrator; request human review

docs.title: 2. Platform Repository Blueprint (thor-agentic-dev)
docs.text:
For clean version control and isolation from production projects, the entire infrastructure lives in a dedicated repository:

thor-agentic-dev/
├── README.md                      # Platform overview & quickstart
├── AGENTS.md                      # Rules of engagement for AI agents
├── .env.example                   # Endpoint URLs and local paths
├── config/
│   ├── models.yaml                # Model definitions, context sizes, quantizations
│   ├── agents.yaml                # Specialist prompts, tool allocations, timeouts
│   ├── permissions.yaml           # Security boundaries and approval gates
│   └── benchmarks.yaml            # 20-task benchmark configurations
├── infrastructure/
│   ├── docker/                    # JetPack 7.x Dockerfiles for Thor
│   ├── systemd/                   # Service definitions for auto-restart
│   ├── networking/                # Firewall, SSH, and tunnel configurations
│   └── monitoring/                # Telemetry collector and logging scripts
├── src/
│   ├── core/                      # Pure domain models (Task, Plan, Diff, Audit)
│   ├── orchestration/             # State machine & repair loop controller
│   ├── model_gateway/             # Unified Ollama / vLLM API client
│   ├── execution/                 # Docker worktree executor
│   ├── adapters/                  # Tool implementations (git, shell, python, stm32, kicad, ros)
│   ├── quality/                   # Automated diff evaluation and test parsers
│   └── observability/             # Health checks and Prometheus/JSON metrics
├── scripts/
│   ├── audit.sh                   # Phase M0 hardware & environment probe
│   ├── install.sh                 # Phase M1 storage & permissions bootstrap
│   ├── start.sh                   # Service launch coordinator
│   └── healthcheck.sh             # API and GPU liveness probe
├── benchmarks/                    # Datasets, runners, and historical results
├── tests/                         # Unit, integration, and security test suites
└── docs/                          # Architecture, installation, and runbooks

docs.title: 3. Formal Implementation Brief for Coding Agents
docs.text:
When deploying an autonomous coding agent (such as Claude Code, OpenCode, or Codex) to build or modify this platform, use the following formal brief:

# Implementation Brief — Thor Agentic Development Platform

## Objective
Build a reproducible, secure, local-first agentic coding platform using an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor as the primary LLM inference server.

The initial execution architecture is hybrid:
- NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor: GPU inference, model storage, API serving, metrics.
- macOS development host: IDE, OpenCode/Claude Code, repositories, local tools.
- Isolated Linux execution containers: builds, tests, and controlled automation.

## Mandatory Implementation Sequence
1. Audit the current Thor hardware and operating system (M0).
2. Validate JetPack, CUDA, Docker, and GPU runtime compatibility (M1).
3. Implement persistent storage, SSH-based access, and health checks (M1).
4. Deploy a supported Ollama inference environment (M2).
5. Validate Qwen3-Coder 30B with real GPU monitoring (M2).
6. Connect OpenCode / Claude Code over a secure SSH tunnel (M3).
7. Create deterministic end-to-end coding-agent tests (M3).
8. Implement a repeatable model benchmarking framework (M4).
9. Evaluate vLLM and optimized model variants with Prefix Caching (M5).
10. Add isolated agent execution and engineering adapters (M6–M7).
11. Implement monitoring, recovery, and operational documentation (M8).

## Architecture Constraints
- Separate domain logic, orchestration, infrastructure, and adapters.
- Use explicit interfaces for model inference and tool execution.
- Never mix incompatible JetPack / CUDA environments.
- Never expose unauthenticated inference APIs to the public internet.
- Never grant agents unrestricted host filesystem or Docker socket access.
- Never auto-flash hardware, release fabrication files, or push protected branches.

## Quality Requirements
- Automated tests where technically applicable.
- Actual execution evidence rather than verbal success claims.
- Explicit PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED status for every milestone.
- An actionable rollback or recovery procedure for every infrastructure change.

docs.title: 4. Recommended Sprint 1 Plan (M0 to M3)
docs.text:
Focus strictly on Sprint 1 (Milestones M0 to M3) before investing effort in multi-agent orchestration or complex GPU optimizations:

  • Step 1: Run hardware and system audit on AGX Thor (audit.sh).
  • Step 2: Verify JetPack 7.x, CUDA 12.8+, and Docker NVIDIA runtime.
  • Step 3: Provision persistent storage under /srv/agentic/.
  • Step 4: Lock down SSH key authentication; disable root and password logins.
  • Step 5: Launch the Ollama Jetson container with GPU offload verified.
  • Step 6: Pull qwen3-coder:30b and confirm 100% GPU offload with nvidia-smi.
  • Step 7: Test inference latency with a test prompt over curl.
  • Step 8: Establish an encrypted SSH tunnel from Mac (localhost:11500 ➔ 127.0.0.1:11434).
  • Step 9: Configure OpenCode v2 or Claude Code on Mac pointing to the tunnel.
  • Step 10: Execute the 6-step MVP test in a designated test repository.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Hands-on exercises. Labs 01–08 take 15–30 minutes each and build on one another, using one practice project throughout: log-summarizer — a small CLI that turns a log file into a Markdown summary. (Use any language you like; Python is assumed in examples.) Lab 09 is standalone: you learn a real topic of your choice.

docs.title: 🏆 Capstone — A Fully Configured Project
docs.text: Build a new small tool from scratch and set up the project the way a professional team would. Suggested topic: a test-report dashboard that turns JUnit XML files into a static HTML page — or pick something from your own work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Build
        P[Plan mode with clarifying questions] --> B[Build with tests]
    end
    subgraph Configure
        C[CLAUDE.md]
        S[settings.json: allow/ask/deny]
        SK[≥1 project skill]
        A[≥1 subagent]
        H[≥2 hooks]
    end
    subgraph Operate
        W[Feature built in a worktree]
        R["/code-review before merge"]
        RT[A routine e.g. weekly dependency check]
    end
    Build --> Configure --> Operate

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Started in Plan mode; plan reviewed and revised once
  • CLAUDE.md with overview, commands, architecture, rules (< 150 lines)
  • .claude/settings.json with sensible allow/ask/deny
  • One project skill (e.g. release-notes)
  • One subagent (e.g. read-only reviewer)
  • Two hooks (e.g. format on edit + notify on stop)
  • One MCP server connected or a documented .mcp.json (e.g. GitHub)
  • One feature developed in a worktree and merged
  • /code-review run and at least one finding fixed
  • One routine created
  • A double-clickable launcher or simple CLI so the tool works without Claude

docs.title: Self-assessment
docs.text:
Question ✔ Can a teammate clone the repo and get the same Claude behavior? Does a fresh session understand the project without exploring? Are secrets impossible for Claude to read? Could you explain each file in .claude/ to someone else?

Use examples/starter-project/ as a reference — not as a copy.

docs.title: Lab 01 — First Project
docs.text: Time: 15 min · Module: 00 Getting Started

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create an empty folder log-summarizer.
  2. Desktop app → Code tab → open the folder (or cd log-summarizer && claude).
  3. Leave model on default, effort on medium, mode on auto.
  4. Run: 
    Initialize a git repository here and create a sample file logs/sample.log
with 50 realistic lines of application logs (INFO/WARN/ERROR, timestamps).
  5. Open the Files panel and the Changed files panel and look at what happened.
  6. Try a follow-up that refines instead of re-prompting: 
    Add 5 more ERROR lines from a "database" component.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• The folder shows up as a project in the sidebar
  • logs/sample.log exists and git is initialized
  • You saw at least one diff in the Changed-files view

docs.title: Reflect
docs.text: Did Claude ask for permission at any point? Why (or why not) in Auto mode?

docs.title: Lab 02 — Plan Mode
docs.text: Time: 30 min · Module: 01 Core Concepts

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Switch mode to Plan.
  2. Send: 
    I want a Python CLI "logsum" that reads a log file and writes a Markdown
summary: counts per level, top 5 error messages, first/last timestamp,
errors per component.

Stack: Python 3.11, standard library only for parsing, pytest for tests,
uv or pip for packaging. Keep the layout small: src/logsum/, tests/.

Before planning, ask me any questions you need.
  3. Answer Claude's questions. Note at least one question you hadn't thought of.
  4. Read the plan. Request one change (e.g. "add a --json output option").
  5. Accept the plan (switches to Auto mode) and let it build.
  6. Run it on logs/sample.log.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• logsum logs/sample.log (or python -m logsum …) prints/writes a summary
  • Tests exist and pass
  • You changed the plan at least once before accepting

docs.title: Stretch
docs.text: Re-run the same build request with effort low in a throwaway folder. Compare speed and quality.

docs.title: Lab 03 — CLAUDE.md
docs.text: Time: 20 min · Module: 02 Project Context

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. In the log-summarizer project run /init.
  2. Open CLAUDE.md. Check: overview, commands, architecture.
  3. Add a Rules section yourself: 
    ## Rules
- Standard library only for parsing; ask before adding dependencies.
- Every new feature needs a pytest test.
- Type hints on all public functions.
  4. Start a new session and ask: "What is this project and how do I run the tests?" — notice Claude answers without searching.
  5. Ask Claude to "remember that I prefer short commit messages". Find out where it stored that (hint: probably not in the repo).
  6. Ask it to store a team decision in the project instead: "Add to CLAUDE.md that timestamps are always ISO 8601 UTC."

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md exists with your Rules section
  • A fresh session answers project questions instantly
  • You know the difference between private memory and project instructions

Compare with examples/starter-project/CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Lab 04 — settings.json
docs.text: Time: 20 min · Module: 02 Project Context

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create a fake secret: echo "API_KEY=do-not-read" > .env and add .env to .gitignore.
  2. Ask Claude: 
    Create .claude/settings.json so that:
- running pytest and the CLI never asks for permission
- installing packages always asks
- .env can never be read
  3. Inspect the file and compare with the example.
  4. Test each rule:
  5. "Run the tests" → no prompt
  6. "Install rich" → you get asked (deny it)
  7. "What's in .env?" → blocked
  8. Add your own spinner verbs for fun.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• All three behaviors verified
  • You can explain the difference between settings.json and settings.local.json

docs.title: Lab 05 — Your First Skill
docs.text: Time: 20 min · Module: 03 Extending Claude

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Ask Claude: 
    Make a global skill called "changelog" that reads git log since the last
tag (or the last 20 commits if there's no tag) and writes a CHANGELOG
entry grouped into Added / Changed / Fixed. Keep the instructions short.
  2. Find it in ~/.claude/skills/changelog/SKILL.md and read it. Improve the description so Claude knows when to use it.
  3. Run /changelog in log-summarizer.
  4. Open a different project and confirm /changelog is available there too.
  5. Now move it into log-summarizer/.claude/skills/. Confirm it disappears from the other project.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• /changelog produces a sensible entry
  • You've seen global vs. project scope in action

docs.title: Stretch
docs.text: Add a scripts/ file to the skill (e.g. a script that finds the last tag) and reference it from SKILL.md.

docs.title: Lab 06 — Subagent
docs.text: Time: 20 min · Module: 03 Extending Claude

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Run /context and note the current usage.
  2. Ask Claude: 
    Create a project subagent "test-gap-finder" (read-only tools, sonnet model)
that reads src/ and tests/ and lists functions without test coverage,
with a suggested test name for each.
  3. Start a new session if it isn't picked up, then: "Use test-gap-finder."
  4. Click the running agent to watch its tool calls.
  5. Run /context again — compare with step 1. The subagent's file reads did not land in your main context.
  6. Ask Claude to write the missing tests based on the report.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• .claude/agents/test-gap-finder.md exists
  • You got a report and your main context stayed small

docs.title: Lab 07 — Hooks
docs.text: Time: 25 min · Module: 03 Extending Claude

docs.title: Part A — "Done" notification
docs.text:
1. Copy examples/starter-project/.claude/hooks/notify.sh (or notify.ps1 on Windows) into log-summarizer/.claude/hooks/.
  2. Add a Stop hook in .claude/settings.json that runs it.
  3. Send "hello" — you should get a desktop notification when Claude finishes. (Check OS notification permissions if not.)

docs.title: Part B — Auto-format on edit
docs.text:
1. Ask Claude: "Add a PostToolUse hook for Edit|Write that runs ruff format on changed Python files." (Install ruff if needed.)
  2. Ask Claude to add a deliberately badly formatted function. Verify it's formatted automatically.

docs.title: Part C — Guardrail
docs.text:
1. Copy block-secrets.sh from the example and wire it as a PreToolUse hook.
  2. Ask "show me .env" — the hook should block it even if settings.json didn't.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• All three hooks fire as expected
  • You can explain why a hook is more reliable than a rule in CLAUDE.md

docs.title: Lab 08 — Parallel Work, Context & Safety Nets
docs.text: Time: 30 min · Module: 04 Daily Workflow

docs.title: Part A — Two sessions, two worktrees
docs.text:
1. Commit everything on main.
  2. Start Session A with worktrees enabled: "Add an --html output option."
  3. Start Session B with worktrees enabled: "Add a --since filter."
  4. Split panes and watch both.
  5. Merge both branches. Resolve conflicts if any (ask Claude to help).

docs.title: Part B — Context hygiene
docs.text:
1. In a long session, run /context.
  2. Run /compact, then /context again.
  3. Run /clear. Note the baseline token count that remains.

docs.title: Part C — Rewind
docs.text:
1. Ask Claude to "rewrite the parser using regex only".
  2. Don't like it? /rewind → pick the prompt before → restore code and conversation.

docs.title: Part D — Review
docs.text: Run /code-review on the merged result. Fix one finding.

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• Both features merged on main
  • You used /compact, /clear, /rewind and /code-review at least once

docs.title: Lab 09 — Learn a Topic with Collect → Understand → Own
docs.text:
Time: 60–90 min · Module: 06 Learning with AI

Pick a topic you actually need. Suggestions: harness vs. loop engineering for agents, MCP security, evaluation of LLM test agents.

docs.title: Part A — Collect (20 min)
docs.text:
1. Fill in research-brief.md with your goal, depth, background and what counts as a good source.
  2. Ask Claude to turn it into a deep-research prompt. Cut at least one part that over-prompts.
  3. Run deep research in your research notebook (e.g. NotebookLM). Delete failed sources.
  4. Export the source list to Markdown and ask Claude to audit it with the audit prompt.
  5. Build a new notebook from the kept sources.

docs.title: Part B — Understand (25 min)
docs.text:
1. Ask Claude for questions based on your goal. Compress them to at most 5.
  2. Ask the notebook each question, one at a time.
  3. Generate one notebook studio output (table or deck) from your answers, not from the whole library.
  4. Ask Claude to reshape your hardest answer into an interactive page around one concrete task of yours.

docs.title: Part C — Own (20 min)
docs.text:
1. Export your questions to questions.md and put them in a folder together with the artifact(s) you want to keep.
  2. Give Claude folder access and use the "job, not structure" prompt from Own. Approve or adjust its plan, then let it build.
  3. Compare the result with examples/learning-archive/.
  4. In a new chat, ask: "What did I learn about ?"

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• Your audit removed or flagged at least one source you wouldn't have caught yourself
  • You have ≤ 5 focused questions with grounded answers
  • One reshaped artifact exists that's specific to your problem
  • A fresh chat can tell you what you learned, show your question path, and link to the notebook

docs.title: Stretch
docs.text: Turn the filing rules into a skill (/file-session) using Module 03, then archive a second session with it.

docs.title: Lab 10 — Ollama & Local Models
docs.text: Time: 20 min · Module: 07 Running with Ollama

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify Ollama & inspect local models on your Mac: 

    ollama --version
ollama list

  2. Launch Claude Code and test --config: Configure or switch your active model: 

    ollama launch claude --config
    Choose a model with tool-calling capabilities (e.g. qwen2.5-coder:8b locally, or a cloud model like gpt-oss:20b-cloud / glm-4.7:cloud).

  3. Check the connection: Inside Claude Code, run: 

    /status
    Confirm that the active model name and the Base URL point to Ollama (http://localhost:11434 or https://ollama.com).

  4. Test the Plan Mode + ASCII Wireframe Prompt: Switch to Plan Mode (Shift + Tab) and test the local model prompt pattern: 

    Design an email verification component. Before generating any HTML or CSS, create a terminal ASCII wireframe in your plan showing the layout, header, logo, call-to-action button, and footer.
    Inspect the ASCII layout before approving code generation.

  5. Test a headless non-interactive command: Exit the session (/exit or Ctrl+C), then run a one-off headless prompt: 

    ollama launch claude --model gpt-oss:20b-cloud --yes -- -p "Count how many markdown files exist in this repo."

  6. Test an in-session /loop: Start an interactive session again and schedule a repeating prompt: 

    /loop 5m Check if git status has changed and print a one-line summary

docs.title: ✅ Done when
docs.text:
• ollama list and /status verify Claude Code is talking to Ollama
  • You switched or selected models using ollama launch claude --config
  • You generated and inspected an ASCII wireframe in Plan Mode before generating code
  • You ran at least one headless command using --yes -- -p
  • You scheduled an in-session loop using /loop

docs.title: Reflect
docs.text:
• Did breaking the prompt into a single component + ASCII wireframe improve the local model's output quality?
  • How did the response speed and VRAM usage on your Mac compare between local 8B models and cloud open models?
